en: *The Record of the Inner Law Sent Back from the Southern Sea*, Scroll One, including the Preface, composed by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Yijing. Yijing’s Preface:

Originally, when the three thousandfold world system first began to be established, the origins of its arising and formation were revealed; once ten billion such systems had been completed, [the Buddha appeared].
There was as yet no order of persons or things.
Since the world was a hollow void, the sun and moon had not yet circulated;
since reality was a profound silence amidst the cycles of sorrow and joy, yin and yang could not be distinguished.

When the beings of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven descended, their bodies were naturally accompanied by radiance. Because they consumed the "earth-fat" (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka), they subsequently gave rise to craving and attachment; they then successively ate forest creepers and fragrant rice, whereupon their bodily radiance gradually faded and the sun and moon first appeared. Thus, the practice of husbandry and the roles of husband and wife arose, while the principles of ruler and subject, father and son, were established.

However, when looking upward at the blue elephant [Mount Sumeru], its wondrous height is suffused with radiant light; when examining downward at the yellow chariot [the earth], it is formed by the agitation of wind and the congealing of water.

Yet to claim that the two polarities (Heaven and Earth) were divided and humans were born within them, spontaneously possessing existence through the resonance of pure and turbid qi, and that Yin and Yang mold all things like a vast furnace or fashion the myriad creatures like clay on a potter’s wheel—this is merely the talk of those who have heard little and speak in fragments.

Thereupon, mountains rose like peaks and stars were scattered across the heavens; sentient beings spread forth and multiplied, resulting in ninety-six divergent paths and twenty-five distinct schools of truth.

The Sāṃkhya school holds that all things begin from the One, while the Vaiśeṣika school maintains that the five destinies arise from six categories. Some bare their shoulders and pluck out their hair, regarding this as the essential means of liberation; others smear their bodies with ash and wear topknots, believing this to be the way to ascend to heaven. Some claim that life arises spontaneously, while others maintain that consciousness must perish at death.
Some say that the realm is profound and obscure, its essence unknowable; others say it is vast and fleeting, its origin beyond comprehension.

Some say that humans constantly obtain the human path; some claim that upon death one immediately becomes a ghost or spirit; others discuss how one does not know whether the butterfly is oneself, nor does one know whether oneself is the form of the butterfly.

Having already become confused by the *guoli* wasp, they further gather their delusions around the *mingle* caterpillar; they compare the primordial chaos (*hundun*) to a chicken egg and remain as dark and obscured as an infant.
Are these not all those who, failing to understand that birth arises from craving and exists by virtue of karma, wander back and forth through the ocean of suffering and the lost ways of saṃsāra?

Thus, it was our Great Master, the World-Honored Śākyamuni, who personally pointed out the level path and embodied the proclamation of the sublime principles; he expounded the twelve links of dependent origination, attained the unique dharmas of the three-sixes, and was titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans and called the All-Knowing One. He led the four types of birth from the burning house and pulled those within the three realms of existence from the city of darkness, enabling them to emerge from the stream of afflictions and ascend to the shore of nirvāṇa.
When he first attained perfect enlightenment, the nine realms of existence on the Dragon River raised their hopes for transcendence;
later, when he shifted his radiance, the six paths at the Deer Park flourished with hearts of refuge.

When the Wheel of Dharma was first turned, five people received transformation; when the traces of the precepts were next discussed, a thousand beings bowed their heads in submission. Thus, he propagated the Brahma-sound in Rājagṛha, where those who attained the fruits of realization were infinite;
he repaid his parental kindness in Kapilavastu, where those who resolved to attain enlightenment were beyond counting.
Beginning with the *Liaojiao* (Teaching of Complete Understanding), he fulfilled his initial vow to manifest his sincerity;
ending with the *Miaoxian* (Sublime Sage), he accords with his later aspiration through the power of his resolve.

He maintained the Dharma for eighty years, extensively saving those in the nine realms of existence; there was no teaching so profound that it was not expounded, and no capacity so subtle that it was not embraced.
If addressed generally to lay followers, one merely speaks briefly of the five prohibitions;
when specifically directed toward the monastic community, one then extensively elucidates the seven categories of offenses.
This is because if one dwells in worldly existence, great transgressions arise, whereas when the precepts flourish, such transgressions are extinguished.
To preserve life is a minor transgression; when the laws are made manifest, the transgression vanishes.

Furthermore, consider how one who harms even a small branch may be reborn among the dragons, while one who compassionately saves a tiny creature’s life ascends together to the imperial abode. Thus, the retribution for good and evil is indeed clear.
Thus, both Sūtra and Śāstra are administered together, and Samādhi and Prajñā are established in tandem; this Tripiṭaka alone is the pivotal cord for gathering in sentient beings.
Subsequently, when one personally encounters the Great Master, the teaching is of a single discourse;
yet, as he rescues beings according to their capacities, the underlying principle leaves no room for alternative interpretations.
When Xue She first took his leave, the Demon King deluded his joyful resolve;
when Xi Lian later proclaimed [the truth], Anuruddha manifested the principle of the cessation of doubt.
It may be said that the conditions for conversion were now exhausted and his great task was fully accomplished.
Consequently, his traces vanished between the two rivers, leaving gods and men with their hopes shrouded;
his shadow sank beneath the twin trees, causing dragons and spirits to break their hearts.
This led to tears falling like mud beside the Śāla grove, and blood flowing like flowering trees around those who wailed.

When the Great Master entered nirvana, the world became empty; subsequently, there arose individuals who propagated the Dharma, leading to five or seven different schools through the process of compilation.
As for the great generals who upheld the Vinaya, their lineages diverged into eighteen distinct sects.

According to what is seen and heard, the three Piṭakas differ in their respective traditions: when putting on the lower garment (*antarvāsa*), the skirt may be worn either slanted or straight; when donning the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), the folds may be narrow or wide.

Regarding cohabitation, staying in separate rooms while corded together is permissible for both parties without fault; regarding the receiving of food, using the hand or drawing a line on the ground are both free from transgression.
Each has its own lineage of transmission, and their practices are not intermingled; the Sarvāstivāda is correct, while the other three are partial.
In the Sarvāstivāda, one must necessarily stay in a separate room, whereas the Saṃmitīya uses a cord to encircle the bed.
The Sarvāstivādins received [the teachings] through oral invitation, while the Mahāsāṃghikas demarcated them by drawing lines on the ground.

As the various schools arose and developed differently, the general outline of their traditions in the Western Regions consists of four primary divisions: First, the Ārya-Mahāsāṃghika-nikāya (translated into Chinese as *Shèng Dàzhòng bù*, the Holy Mahāsāṃghika School). Seven sub-schools branched out from this, and each of their Tripiṭakas contains one hundred thousand verses; in Chinese translation, these would amount to approximately one thousand fascicles.

Second, the Ārya-Sthavira-nikāya (translated into Chinese as *Shèng Shàngzuò bù*, the Holy Sthavira School). Three sub-schools branched out from this, and the extent of their Tripiṭakas is roughly the same as mentioned above.

3. The Ārya-mūla-sarvāstivāda-nikāya, translated into Chinese as the Holy Root Sarvāstivāda School, which branched into four sub-sects; its Tripitaka is approximately the same volume as the former. 4.
The Ārya-sammitīya-nikāya, translated into Chinese as the Holy Saṃmitīya School, which branched into four sub-sects; its Tripitaka consists of three hundred thousand verses.
However, the traditions transmitted by the various schools contain many similarities and differences; for now, I shall speak of their eighteen divisions based on extant facts.
These are further divided into five schools, which have not been heard of in the Western Regions.
In the interim, regarding their divisions, origins, disappearances, and specific sectarian names, the details are not uniform as discussed elsewhere; thus, they shall not be described here at length.

Consequently, throughout the lands of the Five Indias and the various islands of the South Seas, all speak of four types of *nikāyas*, though the number of those held in high esteem varies from place to place.
In Magadha, all four schools are studied, with the Sarvāstivāda being the most prevalent.
In the country of Sindhu in Western India, known as Rota, three schools are practiced to a lesser extent, though the Sammitīya is particularly numerous there.
In the north, all follow the Sarvāstivāda school, though occasionally they encounter members of the Mahāsāṃghika.
To the south, everyone adheres to the Sthavira school, while other sects exist only in small numbers.

As for the various kingdoms of the eastern frontiers, four schools are practiced in a mixed fashion; traveling five hundred stations east from Nālandā, these are all termed the eastern frontiers, extending as far as the Great Black Mountains (Mahākāla-parvata), which are estimated to lie on the southern border of Tibet.
According to tradition: traveling southwest from this region for over a month, one reaches this mountain range.

To the south of this, bordering the edge of the sea, lies the kingdom of Śrīkṣetra; to the southeast is the kingdom of Laṅkaśū; to the east is the kingdom of Sāmbhadraka; and further east, reaching its limit, is the kingdom of Lin-yi. All of these nations most strictly revere the Triple Gem, and there are many who observe the precepts. Begging for alms and practicing *dhūta* austerities is the established custom of these countries.
In the West, it is seen that [the Sammitīya school] truly stands apart from the common ranks.
Throughout the continent of Siṃhala (Lion Island), everyone is an Elder (Sthavira), yet the Great Assembly (Mahāsāṃghika) rejects them.

However, there are more than ten kingdoms in the various islands of the South Sea where the Mūlasarvāstivāda school alone prevails; the Saṃmitīya is highly esteemed there. Recently, two other schools have begun to appear alongside it. Counting from the west, there are the island of Bharuśa and the island of Malaya, which is the present-day kingdom of Śrīvijaya.

There are Mahāśina Island, Haling Island, Da-da Island, Pen-pen Island, Bali Island, Jue-lun Island, Fo-shi-bu-la Island, A-xian Island, and Mo-jia-man Island; furthermore, there are smaller islands that cannot be recorded in full. All of these follow the Buddha-dharma, and for the most part they adhere to the Hīnayāna;
only in Melayu is there a small amount of the Mahāyāna.
The perimeters of these various countries may be a hundred *li*, several hundred *li*, or perhaps a hundred *yi*;
although the great ocean is difficult to measure in *li*, one may infer it by the strings of merchant ships, which serves as a reliable standard.
When [the author] first arrived in Jiaoguang, he consequently referred to them all as people of the country of Kunlun.

Only these Kunlun people have curled hair and dark complexions; the inhabitants of all other countries do not differ from those of the Divine Land (China). They go barefoot and wear *gànmàn* (loincloths), which is their universal custom, as described in detail in the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas).
From Huánzhōu, traveling due south on foot for more than half a month, or by boat for only five or six days, one arrives at Bǐjǐng.
Continuing south to Zhānpō is Línyì.
In this country, the Saṃmitīya school predominates, while the Sarvāstivāda is present only in small numbers.

Traveling southwest for one month, one reaches the kingdom of Bāman (formerly known as Fúnán). This was originally a land of the naked; its people mostly worshipped the gods, but later the Buddha-dharma flourished there.
However, an evil king has now exterminated them all, so that monks are entirely absent and only heterodox practitioners dwell there in a mixed fashion.
This is precisely the southern corner of Jambudvīpa, not a sea-island.

Nevertheless, regarding the general framework of the Eastern Land (China), the Dharmaguptaka school is largely practiced; in various regions of Guanzhong, the Mahāsāṃghika school was formerly prevalent, while in Jiangnan and the regions beyond the ridges, the Sarvāstivāda school flourished first. As for those who speak of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, these titles were mostly adopted from the scriptural fascicles themselves to serve as their headings.

Upon careful examination of the differences between the four schools, their systems of discipline (*vinaya*) are distinct; their gravity and lightness are vastly separated, and their permissions and prohibitions are far apart, with members of the monastic community each relying upon the tenets of their own school.

It is not appropriate to substitute one’s own grave rules with the minor matters of others, or to employ the texts of one’s own school while finding fault with the regulations of others; for if this were so, the principle of distinct schools would not be established, and the logic of permitting or prohibiting would remain undifferentiated—how could one person possibly practice all four traditions simultaneously?

The parable of the torn garment and the golden staff illustrates that the realization of cessation is not different [among the schools]; those who practice the Dharma must rely upon their own respective sects. King Bimbisāra saw in a dream a single piece of cloth torn into eighteen fragments, and a golden staff cut into eighteen sections.
Terrified, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"More than one hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a King Aśoka whose majesty shall extend over Jambudvīpa."
"At that time, although the monks were divided into eighteen schools, their aim toward the gate of liberation was one and the same.
This was a premonitory sign; may Your Majesty not be distressed by it."
Among these four divisions, the distinction between Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna is not fixed.

In the regions of Northern India and Southern Sea, they practice exclusively Hīnayāna; in the lands of China and the Red District (Zhōngguó), their intent lies in the Mahāyāna teachings; and in all other places, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are practiced together.

Examining their ultimate aim, however, the legal regulations do not differ; both systems consist of five chapters and universally cultivate the Four Noble Truths. If one pays homage to Bodhisattvas and recites Mahāyāna sūtras, it is termed "Great";
if one does not perform these practices, it is designated as "Small."
Regarding what is called the Mahāyāna, there are no more than two types:

first, Madhyamaka; second, Yogācāra. In Madhyamaka, conventional phenomena exist while their ultimate nature is emptiness, being as illusory as a phantom; in Yogācāra, there is nothing external and all internal phenomena are consciousness-only.
Both strictly adhere to the sacred teachings; which is right and which is wrong?
Since we all share the same commitment to nirvana, what is true and what is false?
Our intention lies in severing afflictions and delusions to rescue sentient beings; how could we wish to cause widespread confusion and further increase their deep-seated fetters?
By practicing accordingly, both ascend to the other shore; by turning one's back on it, both drown in the flow of birth and death.
In the Western lands, these two practices proceed together without contradiction or rivalry; yet, lacking the eye of wisdom, who can discern right from wrong?
If one were to practice this through long-standing habituation, it would be fortunate indeed that one need not undergo the hardship of self-denial.

Furthermore, regarding the observance of the Vinaya in the Divine Land (China), the various schools have influenced one another; consequently, the masters who lecture and compile texts have resulted in commentaries and digests that are overly complex and disordered. Thus, the five categories and seven groups of offenses become easier in some places yet more difficult in others, and the methods for avoiding or committing infractions appear only to vanish again. This has led those of superior capacity to lose heart after covering but a single basketful of earth, and those of middling or inferior capacity to turn back from their studies after hearing but a single session, such that even those among the elite with graying beards have failed to achieve their goal, let alone those of middle or lower standing who reach white-haired old age.

The root texts of the Vinaya are naturally obscure; one may spend a lifetime reading the commentaries as master and disciple transmit them as established precedents. When discussing the sections of the chapters, they are divided and further subdivided; when describing the determination of offenses, they are analyzed down to the individual phrases and even the constituent words.
Examining its merit, it truly involves the labor of constructing a mountain;
scrutinizing its benefit, it occasionally possesses the moisture of a sea pearl.

Furthermore, since the intent of all those who compose works is to make them easy for others to understand, how could one deliberately employ esoteric language and further create parodies to explain them?
It is like water overflowing from level plains and rushing into a deep well; those who intend to drink and quench their thirst find no way to save their lives.

If one were to follow the Vinaya texts literally, it would not be so; yet in adjudicating the gravity of offenses, one need only employ a few lines of text, and explaining the expedient means for committing an offense does not require half a day. This is the great consensus among the followers of the Dharma in the Western Regions and the South Seas.

As for the land of the Divine Continent (China), where rites and instruction flourish: people revere and serve their sovereigns and parents; they honor and yield to their elders; they are frugal, pure, humble, and compliant; they take only after acting with righteousness; they are filial sons and loyal ministers, being careful of their persons and moderate in their expenditures.
The Emperor nurtures the myriad subjects with benevolence, his compassionate concern for those within the moats manifesting from the break of dawn;
and the assembly of ministers, none of whom fail to stand with hands folded, present their resolve throughout the night as if treading upon thin ice.

At times, he extensively inaugurated the Three Vehicles and broadly opened a hundred seats; he established caityas across the eight marshes, so that all who possess discernment turned their hearts toward him;
he dispersed monasteries throughout the nine realms, so that all those lost on the path were led to turn their aspirations [toward enlightenment].

Magnificent were the farmers’ songs amidst the furrows, and dignified were the merchants’ chants upon their boats and carriages. Consequently, the kingdom of Kīṭa-raja (Chicken-Precious), where elephants are honored, bowed its head at the vermilion steps; and the regions of Suvarṇabhūmi (Golden Neighbor) and Vajraparvata (Jade Ridge) offered their sincerity at the azure courtyard. To practice non-action and attend to no affairs—this is indeed unsurpassed. As for Kīṭa-raja, it is the Western name for the country of Goryeo, known as Kukkuṭa-sailendra.
*Ku-k'u-t'a* means "chicken," and *shuo-lo* means "noble.
According to Western traditions, that country venerates the chicken, regarding it as divine and worthy of honor; therefore, they wear its feathers as ornaments.
Regarding the term "Eminent Elephant" (Xiàng-zūnzhě): in the kingdoms of the West, the elephant is considered supreme, and this is likewise the case throughout the Five Indies.

As for the ritual protocols of these monastic companions when preaching, their disciples remain solemn and revere the ultimate meaning with the utmost sincerity. Having retired to dwell in secluded valleys and cast off the cage of worldly entanglements, they rinse their mouths at mountain streams while contemplating the distant, and sit amidst the thickets of the forest to settle their aspirations. By practicing the Path during the six periods of the day, they are able to repay the kindness of those who offer pure faith; by entering meditative concentration twice daily, they are worthy of receiving the veneration of both devas and humans.
This is in perfect accord with the sūtras and vinaya; what fault could there be?

Nevertheless, due to errors in oral transmission, discrepancies in ritual protocols, and the naturalization of long-standing habits, there have been instances that deviate from the fundamental principles. Therefore, I have respectfully relied upon the holy teachings and the currently practiced essential rules to compile a total of forty chapters, divided into four fascicles, titled the *Nanhai Jiguinei Fa Zhuan* (Record of the Inner Dharma Sent Back from the South Seas).

Furthermore, one scroll of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Tang in the Western Regions* (*Da Tang Xiyu Gaoseng Zhuan*), along with various sūtras and śāstras, have all been recorded and appended here for the sake of returning [to the source].

I pray that the virtuous ones will give rise to the resolve to propagate the Dharma, eschew notions of "self" and "other," and skillfully measure their conduct in accordance with the Buddha's teachings; do not disparage others simply because you hold the Dharma in high esteem.

However, while the principles of the sutras and śāstras transmitted through antiquity and the present are well-versed in the Chan gate, the subtle nuances of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are difficult to explain exhaustively here. For now, I shall briefly set forth the methods of practice in accordance with the Vinaya regulations to present them first, fully enumerating the articles and precepts to examine the traditions of the masters in authentic records.
Even if my life should sink with the evening light, I hope to achieve the merit of a single basketful of earth;
even if the flame should be extinguished by the morning glow, I pray that there may be a succession of a hundred lamps.
By reading this, one need not labor a single step to traverse the Five Indias upon a short flight of stairs.
Before a single inch of time has passed, you have truly reflected upon the deluded tracks of a thousand years.

I pray that you will examine the Tripiṭaka, stirring the ocean of Dharma to raise its four waves; clarify the five sections [of the Vinaya], launching the vessel of wisdom to rescue the six classes of beings.

Although I have personally received the master’s instructions and thoroughly examined the profound mysteries, I fear that unless these insights are brought forth from a mind of skillful artistry, I shall ultimately be ridiculed by those with the eye of wisdom. This is all I have to say.

The forty offenses incurred by those of ancient virtue were not committed as ordinary people;
all that is discussed here is based on the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, and one must not intermingle the matters of other schools with this.
This is largely consistent with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Regarding the divisions of the Sarvāstivāda school, there are three distinct sects:
first, Dharmaguptaka; second, Mahīśāsaka; and third, Kāśyapīya.
None of these practices were observed throughout the five regions of India; they existed only sporadically in the kingdom of Uddiyāna, as well as in Kucha and Khotan.
Furthermore, even the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) is not a text of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school.
1. Breaking the Summer Retreat is Not Being a Minor: Regarding all bhikṣus who have broken the summer retreat, they simply do not obtain its ten benefits;
however, this remains their original status, and in principle, there is no reason for them to become "minors."
How can it be permissible that one who was previously honored now, in turn, pays homage to those of lower status?

This practice has become a custom without any scriptural basis; by accepting invitations according to the Indian [summer] calendar, the fault of theft may arise. Therefore, one ought to investigate and deliberate with care.

In principle, there must be no negligence; one should appropriately determine seniority based on the date of receiving the precepts. Even if one has lost a summer retreat, one should not be relegated to a lower rank.
Upon examining the sacred teachings, there is no such text; who in the past ever authorized this practice?

2. Etiquette for Facing the Honored One: Regarding etiquette for facing the Honored One, it follows the Buddhist tradition; when facing an image or being near a venerable teacher, one should remain barefoot unless ill—there is no allowance for wearing shoes or sandals.
One should habitually travel elsewhere with the right shoulder bared, the left shoulder covered by the robe, and the head uncovered by a turban or cloth; this is the standard practice.

There is no fault in deviating from this when in a place where it is not the custom. In cold countries, one is permitted to wear short boots, and other types of footwear may be used as appropriate for each location.

Subsequently, as distant lands and foreign regions differ in their climates of cold and heat, there are many instances where local practices deviate from the holy teachings; in principle, it is permissible to temporarily wear [additional clothing] for the sake of bodily sustenance during the months of midwinter, but during the spring and summer, one must strictly adhere to the Vinaya regulations.
The prohibition against wearing sandals while circumambulating a Buddhist stupa was already clearly established in the teachings;
the ban on wearing leather boots within the incense altar has been promulgated for a long time.
Yet, those who willfully contravene these rules are merely acting with arrogant defiance toward the golden words of the Buddha.

3. Eating while Seated on Small Stools. Regarding the practice of eating while seated on small stools: when the Western Sangha is about to take their meal, everyone must first wash their hands and feet thoroughly. Each person sits individually upon a small stool—approximately seven inches high and one chi square—woven from rattan cords, with rounded legs and light in weight.
Those of lower or junior status may use smaller ones according to the occasion.

With both feet planted on the ground, a basin and bowl were placed before him; the floor was smeared clean with cow dung and fresh leaves were spread upon it. His seat was one cubit away from the others so that they did not touch, for I have never seen anyone sit cross-legged upon a large bed while eating.

Furthermore, according to the sacred regulations, the length of a bed is eight finger-breadths of the Buddha; tripling this results in twenty-four finger-breadths of a person of medium height, which corresponds to one and a half *chi* of the *hu* (official's tablet) measure.
In the various monasteries of the Eastern Land (China), the height of the beds exceeds two chi; this is fundamentally improper for sitting, as it carries the fault of using high beds.
Since the entire community conforms to this practice, what can be done?
Those who protect against transgressions must observe the standard measurements.
Now, the four meditation seats at Lingyan are one chi high; there is indeed a profound reason for this being the design established by the ancient masters.
For instance, sitting in a row with legs crossed and knees pressed together while eating is not the original method; you should take note of this.

I have heard that when the Buddha-dharma first arrived, the monks all sat in a squatting posture while eating; it was not until the Jin dynasty that this practice fell into disuse, and from that time onward, they have eaten while sitting in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

However, since the holy teachings arrived in the East nearly seven hundred years ago, ten dynasties have passed, each producing its own eminent figures. As Indian monks have successively come to China, Chinese masters have stood shoulder to shoulder receiving their instruction; some even traveled to the Western Regions in person to witness the truth and falsehoods for themselves. Yet, though they returned to report what they had seen, who was able to put their words into practice?

Furthermore, a sutra states, "Having finished eating, he washed his feet," which clarifies that he was not sitting on a bed; since the vegetable food was discarded at the edge of his feet, we know that sitting with the legs hanging down is the correct practice.
A disciple of the Buddha ought to emulate the Buddha; even if one cannot follow his example, one must not treat it with derision or laughter.
This is because sitting upon a spread cloth makes it difficult to maintain ritual purity, and one cannot avoid the defilement of leftover food or improper contact.

Furthermore, to collect the remaining food from the assembly is deeply contrary to proper decorum; to remove it would instead defile the monks' bowls, and for family members to then handle clean vessels is a hollow pretense of protecting purity, the efficacy of which has not yet been seen.
I hope you will examine this thoroughly and consider both its advantages and disadvantages. 4.

The Fourfold Division of Food into Pure and Touched: Generally, regarding the methods of eating for monastics and laypeople in the West (India), there are distinct rules concerning what is pure and what is touched; once a single mouthful has been consumed, it all becomes "touched" (impure).
The vessels used should not be carried away; place them by your side and discard them all together once you have finished.

Any remaining food should be given to those who may eat it; it is certainly improper to collect it again. Whether one is noble or humble, this rule is the same for all. This is a celestial custom, not merely a human practice.

Therefore, various treatises state: "To not chew tooth-sticks, to not wash after defecating or urinating, and to eat food without the distinction between pure and impure contact is considered contemptible. How could one take back and serve again food that has already become impure through contact; return leftover food to the kitchen; pour remaining cakes back into the storage jar; put long-simmered broth back into the cauldron; eat soup and vegetables again the following morning; or still consume cakes and fruit on a subsequent day?
Those who uphold the Vinaya clearly understand the distinctions between what is permissible and what is not, whereas those who follow common practice treat everything with indiscriminate uniformity.

Furthermore, regarding the acceptance of offerings for the *poṣadha* or other food and drink, once they have entered the mouth, they immediately become "tainted" (*sappāṇaka*). Only after rinsing the mouth with pure water may one then touch others or other pure food.
If one touches another person without having first washed and rinsed one's mouth, both parties become impure; the person who was touched must likewise rinse their mouth for purification.
If one touches a dog or a canine, one must also wash and rinse one's mouth.

The person who tastes the food should stand to one side; having finished tasting it, they must wash their hands, rinse their mouth, and cleanse the tasting utensils before touching the cauldron or pot.
If this is not done, the prayers offered and the ritual prohibitions will have no efficacy, and even if offerings are presented, the deities will not accept them.

Speaking from this perspective, whatever offerings one prepares—whether intended for presentation to the Triple Gem, for veneration of spirits and deities, or as ordinary meals—all must be pure and clean.
If one has not yet purified oneself through bathing and rinsing, or has not washed after the evacuation of excrement or urine, it is entirely improper to consume food.

In common parlance it is also said: "Only after a pure fast does one perform the ritual sacrifice to the sages; when clipping one's nails, they should be cut close to the skin; casting off worldly delusions, one follows the path of Confucius and Yan Hui. Such sayings as these likewise indicate that matters must be kept clean, and that offerings should not be made with leftover food.

Whenever vegetarian offerings or the regular meals for the Sangha are prepared, they must be supervised. If one fears that the time will pass once the meal is finished, then regardless of whether one is a monastic or a layperson, one may take a portion and eat it first even before the offering has been presented; this is permitted by the Buddha and carries no fault.
Recently, I have observed that when monks and nuns assist in administrative oversight, they often eat past noon; thus, they incur transgressions despite their merit, which is not appropriate.
However, the reason why the land of the Five Indias is said to differ from other nations lies precisely in this foundation of purity and defilement.

In the past, an envoy from the northern lands of the Hu traveled to the Western Kingdoms and was frequently ridiculed by the people. This was primarily because he did not wash after using the toilet and left leftover food in his basin; furthermore, during meals, he sat in a crowded cluster, jostling one another, showing no avoidance of pigs or dogs, and failing to chew tooth-sticks—consequently inviting widespread derision and criticism.
Therefore, those who practice the Dharma must exercise the utmost care and not treat this matter lightly.

However, in the Eastern Land (China), it has long been the case that food is consumed without the distinction between the pure and the defiled; despite hearing these teachings, most have yet to grasp their proper application. Were it not for personal instruction, one would be unable to achieve true understanding.

5. Removing Impurities after Eating: At the time of finishing a meal, one should either use a vessel to receive [the water], or go to a secluded place, or toward a drain, or stand at the edge of a step. Whether holding a flask oneself or having someone else provide the water, one must wash the hands thoroughly; the mouth must chew a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) to clean the teeth and scrape the tongue, ensuring complete cleanliness. If residual saliva remains, the fast (*upavāsa*) is not accomplished.
Thereafter, using bean dregs or sometimes earth mixed with water, he kneads them into a paste to wipe his lips and mouth, ensuring they are free of oily residue.
Next, he takes water from a pure flask, holding it in a conch-shell cup, or using fresh leaves, or receiving it directly in his hands.
The vessel and the hands must be scrubbed clean with three types of powder—bean dregs, soil, and dried cow dung—to wash away all grease.

If one is in a secluded place, one may pour water from a clean jar directly into the mouth; however, if one is in a public area, there are prohibitions in the Vinaya, and one must rinse two or three times before purity is achieved.
Prior to this point, it is improper to swallow the saliva in the mouth; once one's dignified demeanor (*vīrya*) has been compromised, every swallow incurs an offense.

Furthermore, until one has rinsed the mouth again with pure water, all spittle and saliva must be discarded outside; if the time passes noon, one further commits the offense of eating at an improper time (*akāla-bhojana*).
This is something few people recognize; even if they do know it, guarding against it is not easy.
Considering this, it is truly difficult to avoid the fault of using bean flour and ash-water, for there remains food stuck between the teeth and grease lingering upon the tongue.

The wise should contemplate this principle and maintain mindfulness; how could one allow conversation to exceed the proper time after a formal meal has concluded? To fail to keep a water vessel for purification or to refrain from chewing tooth-sticks, thereby retaining impurities throughout the day and inviting transgressions all night long—by such means to reach the end of life would surely be difficult.
It is also the proper ritual for him to have a disciple carry and present the water from the purification flask (*śodhanī-ghaṭa*).

Regarding the two flasks of water, there are two flasks for each of the two types of water; generally, water is divided into pure (*viśuddha*) and defiled (*sāṃsṛṣṭa*), and there are two flasks [for these].
Those for the pure (śuddha) are made entirely of earthenware or porcelain; those for the impure (āśuci) may also include copper or iron.
The pure are intended for drinking at improper times; the impure are required for the needs of defecation and urination.
The pure must be held only after washing the hands and must be placed in a clean location.
As for the *spraṣṭavya* (touch), it is that which the hand grasps; it may be placed wherever it is touched.
Only water contained in this pure flask or in a new, pure vessel may be drunk outside of the proper time.
That which is contained in other vessels is called "timely water" (*kālodaka*). Drinking it before midday is without fault; however, if one drinks it after noon, there is an offense.

As for the method of making the flask (*karakam*), the lid must be joined to the mouth, with a pointed spout protruding from the top about two finger-widths high. A small hole should be bored through it, as thick as a copper chopstick, through which one may drink the water.

On the side, a separate circular hole should be opened; it should be enclosed so that it stands upright with a height of two finger-widths, and the hole should be about the size of a coin. Water should be added at this point.
It should hold two or three *sheng*; a smaller vessel would be of no use.
Fearing that insects or dust might enter these two openings, one may place a lid upon them, or use bamboo, wood, cloth, or leaves to wrap and block them.
A Brahman monk there took this instruction and fashioned such covers.
When drawing water, one must wash the interior until all dust and grime are removed before beginning to take in fresh water.

How can it be permitted to keep only a single small copper vessel for water without distinguishing between pure and defiled, merely placing a lid on it and inserting a spout so that when water is poured out it flows in a scattered manner, making it unfit for use and impossible to distinguish purity from defilement?
If there is grime or a foul odor within the vessel, it is unfit for holding water; even a single *śu* or two *he* will fail to serve its purpose in every respect.

Regarding the method for making the water-bag (*kamaṇḍalu-paṭa*): one should take a piece of cloth approximately two *zhì* long and one *zhì* wide, fold both ends together at the corners and sew them closed. At each of the two corners, attach a single strap just one *zhé* in length. Place the bottle inside and carry it over the shoulder.
The alms-bowl bag is likewise shaped in this manner: it covers the mouth of the bowl so that dust and soil do not enter, and because its base is pointed, the bowl does not shift or turn.
The bag for storing the bowl differs from this, as described elsewhere.

Placing all his alms bowls and personal garments upon one shoulder, with the *kāṣāya* robe draped over both, he proceeded holding a parasol; these are all the ritual observances for those who have left the household life according to the Buddha’s teaching.

Those with leisure carry the *spraśa-bhājana* (touch-vessel) and a leather sandal bag in their hands, while holding the mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*) slanted across their bodies; their movements are composed and dignified, fittingly illustrated by the "Bird Simile" and the *Candraprabha-sūtra*.

As for the Bodhi tree at the Royal City, Vulture Peak, the Deer Park, the site of the Śāla trees where the Crane Transformation occurred, and the desolate place of the Magpie Mound—whenever they perform prostrations before the *caityas*, people from all four directions gather there, and every day thousands observe this very same custom.
If the virtuous masters of Nālandā Monastery, who are all deeply learned, travel by carriage, none of them ride on saddled horses.
This is likewise the case for those of the Great King’s Monastery; all their requisites are carried by men, or they are held up by young boys.
This is the monastic protocol of the Western [tradition].
7. Morning Inspection for Insects: Every morning one must inspect water.
Water is categorized as being from jars, wells, ponds, or rivers; the methods of inspection vary accordingly.
Once dawn has broken, first observe the water in the flask.

One may pour a handful of it into a clean white copper cup, a copper plate, a conch-shell cup, or a lacquered vessel, and place it upon a brick; or one may prepare a separate wooden device for observing the water, holding it with the hand over the mouth and gazing at it for a long while, or one may also observe it within a basin or jar.
If there are insects even as small as the tip of a hair, one must maintain mindfulness.
If insects are seen, pour the contents back into the bottle, then wash the vessel again and again with fresh water until it is free of insects before ceasing.
Where there is a pond or river, one should take a water jar to that place, pour out the water containing insects, and filter fresh, pure water.
If there is only a well, one should filter it according to the rule.
If one observes the well water, when drawing water, one should take a handful from within the water jar using a copper cup and examine it as described above.
If there are no insects, one may use the water throughout the night; if there are, it must be filtered as before.
Regarding the inspection of water from ponds and rivers, the details are as explained in the Vinaya.

As for those who filter water, in the Western Regions (India) they use fine white cotton cloth, while in the Eastern Lands (China) it is appropriate to use fine silk, either rubbed with rice or slightly boiled.
If it is raw silk, small insects will pass straight through.
One may take four chi of boiled silk, grasp the edges and pull them taut, then fold and pleat both ends together and stitch them so they adhere; this is the pattern for gauze.

The two corners are provided with straps, and two side-ropes are placed at the flanks; a horizontal bar is positioned in the center, spanning sixteen inches when extended. The two ends are tied to pillars, and basins are placed beneath to catch the water. When pouring water, the bottom of the jar must enter within the strainer.
If it were otherwise, the insects would fall with the water; whether they fell to the ground or into the basin, they would still not escape being killed.
Whenever water first enters the filter, one must take it up and examine it; if there are insects, one must change the water immediately, but if it is pure, one may use it as usual.

Once the water is sufficient, one may turn over the strainer. Two people each grasp one end of the strainer and turn it over to place it inside the vessel for releasing living beings. Pour water over it three times, and further rinse the exterior with water. Place water inside again to catch and observe [the insects]; if there are no insects, one may set aside the strainer as desired.
This water must be re-examined after having stood overnight.
Regarding any water that has been left over for a night and is not inspected in the morning—whether it contains insects or not—the Vinaya states that using it will incur an offense.

However, there are many different methods for obtaining water while protecting living beings; among these, the use of this filter is most essential at wells. At ponds or rivers, one may instead install a roll-up filter or use an *āyambila* (inversion) vessel to provide temporary relief.

Furthermore, in the sixth and seventh months, these insects become even finer than at other times; they can pass straight through ten layers of raw silk. Those who delight in protecting living beings should, as a matter of course, maintain mindfulness and employ skillful means to ensure they avoid harm.

Alternatively, one may use a ceramic basin or a strainer, which are also economical and practical; however, monasteries in the Western regions mostly use copper, as these are all established by the Holy One, and thus their significance must not be underestimated.

As for the vessel for releasing living beings, fashion a small water jar with a wide-open mouth; attach two handles to its sides so that a double-rope may be lowered into the water, inverted, and pulled out after being submerged two or three times.

If it is a water filter belonging to a monastery, the ordained monks are fundamentally not permitted to touch it; the same applies to the water within the room at all times—it may only be drunk after one who has not yet received full ordination takes it up.
Regarding those who drink at improper times, they must use purified cloths, purified bottles, and purified vessels before it is fit for consumption.

Abstaining from taking life is a natural precept (*dharmatā-śīla*); among those to be guarded, it is grave and stands at the head of the ten non-virtuous actions, making it logically impossible to treat it with negligence.
The water filter is counted among the six essential items and must therefore be carried.
If one travels even three or five li, one should not go without it.

If you know that a monastery does not filter its water, it is improper to eat or drink there; that one might die of thirst on a long journey is sufficient as a warning, so how can you ever allow yourself to use water without ever examining it?
Although there are strainers, insects still die inside them; even if one wishes to save them, few understand the proper ritual.
Placing the strainer upside down over the mouth of a well shows no understanding of the vessel for releasing living beings; even if it reaches the water, there is no doubt that the insects will die.

At that time, there were those who made small circular strainers, barely large enough to hold one *sheng* or two *he*, made of coarse, thin silk; they did not originally intend to observe insects, merely hanging them beside their bowls so that others might see them. Lacking any intention to protect life, they incurred transgressions day after day, yet masters and disciples passed this practice down to one another as a transmission of the Dharma.
How truly lamentable! How deeply one must sigh with sorrow!
As for the water vessel, every person should maintain their own; a jar for releasing living beings must be present everywhere.

Regarding the chewing of tooth-sticks: one must chew a tooth-stick every morning at dawn to scrub the teeth and scrape the tongue, ensuring it is done according to the Dharma. Only after rinsing and cleansing oneself thoroughly should one perform acts of reverence.
If it were otherwise, both the one receiving the prostration and the one prostrating to another would all incur offense.
As for the tooth-stick, in Sanskrit it is called *dantakāṣṭha*; *danta* is translated as "tooth," and *kāṣṭha* is simply "wood."

It should be twelve finger-widths long and no shorter than eight finger-widths; its thickness should be like that of a small finger, with one end tapered. One must chew it thoroughly for a long time and then clean one's teeth and gums thoroughly.
If one is in close proximity to a person of honor, one should cover the mouth with the left hand.
Having finished using it, one should break it apart, bend it, and use it to scrape the tongue; alternatively, one may use a separate tongue-scraper made of copper or iron.

Alternatively, take a thin slice of bamboo or wood about the size of a small finger's surface; with one end tapered for cleaning between the teeth, bend it to scrape the tongue, taking care not to cause injury.
Once you have finished using it, you may wash it together with [the water] and discard it in a secluded place.

Whenever discarding tooth-sticks, spitting water from the mouth, or blowing one's nose or saliva, one must snap the fingers three times, or otherwise clear the throat twice; if one does not do so, there is an offense in discarding them.
One may use large logs that have been split, or small strips cut from branches.

For those near mountain retreats, acorn-wood branches and kudzu vines are best; for those in level fields, paper mulberry, peach, locust, or willow may be used as desired. These should be collected in advance and prepared so that there is no lack when needed.
That which is moist must be received from another; that which is dry is permitted to be held by oneself.
Those who are young and strong may take it up and chew it at will; those who are elderly and infirm should strike it with the head [of a pestle] to crush it.
For the wood strips, those that are bitter, astringent, and pungent are preferred; those that form a fibrous mass when chewed at the tip are the best.

The coarse *hú* leaf root is extremely refined—specifically the root of *cāng'ěr* (mushroom) taken from a depth of two inches underground—it strengthens the teeth, freshens the breath, aids digestion, and eliminates phlegm. If used for half a month, bad breath will suddenly disappear; toothache and dental fatigue will be cured within thirty days.
One must chew thoroughly and cleanse the teeth until saliva and phlegm flow out, then rinse with plenty of water; this is the method.
Subsequently, if one can drink a single handful of water through the nose, this is the technique of Nāgārjuna for longevity.
If one’s nose does not become congested, drinking from it is also excellent; by using it for a long time, one will have few illnesses.

However, the roots of the teeth harbor long-standing impurities that harden over time; these must be scraped away completely. By rinsing and gargling thoroughly, they will not decay further, and toothache will naturally cease for the rest of one's life. In the Western Regions, such dental pain is entirely unknown, which is truly due to the chewing of *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks).
How could it be permissible not to recognize that *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-stick) is called "willow branch"?
Willow trees are extremely rare in the Western Regions, yet the translators arbitrarily transmitted this designation;
the Buddha’s *dantakāṣṭha* tree is truly not a willow, as I personally observed for myself at Nālandā Monastery.
Since this cannot be trusted by others, those who hear it need not trouble themselves with confusion.
Checking the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it says: "It was at the time of chewing the tooth-stick."

Furthermore, some use slender willow twigs, chewing five or six whole pieces within the mouth without rinsing them out; others swallow the juice, believing it to be a means of eliminating disease. Thus, they seek purity but instead incur filth; they hope to dispel illness but instead invite affliction.
There may be those who are unaware of this, yet it does not fall within the scope of our current discussion.

However, according to the laws of the Five Indias, chewing a tooth-stick is a constant daily practice; even three-year-old children are taught to do so from the outset, as both the sacred teachings and secular customs find mutual benefit therein.
Having thus expressed praise and blame, one should practice equanimity according to the mind.

9. The Rules for Receiving the Upavāsa Fast. Ninth: The Rules for Receiving the Upavāsa Fast. Generally speaking, regarding the methods for responding to invitations in the Western Regions as well as the various kingdoms of the South Sea, I shall briefly set forth their ritual protocols.
In the Western Regions, the donor first pays homage to invite the monks; on the day of the feast, he comes to announce that the time has arrived.

The vessels and seats of the monastic community are measured according to the requirements of the occasion; they may be carried by lay attendants (*karmadāna*) or received from others as pure objects. As for the vessels, they are exclusively of a single color—copper—and must be scrubbed clean with powdered ash.
The seats are each individual small stools; they should not be joined together so that they touch one another. The rules for these stools have already been explained in Chapter Three.

As for earthenware vessels that have never been used before, using them once incurs no fault; however, once they have been used, they should be discarded in a pit or trench, as they have become defiled and must not be collected again.
Therefore, along the roadsides of Western countries (India), the discarded vessels at places where alms-food is provided are as high as mountains, yet they are never used again.
This is just like the earthenware vessels in Xiangyang, which are collected after use; had they been discarded there, it would have been equivalent to violating the rules of purity.
Furthermore, ceramic and lacquerware were originally unknown in the Five Indies; if ceramic is coated with oil, it is undoubtedly pure.
As for lacquer vessels, even when merchants occasionally bring them to the West or the South Seas, they are never used for eating, precisely because they retain grease.
If it is indeed new, wash it with clean ashes until the oily odor is removed; in that case, its use should be permissible.
As for wooden vessels that were not originally intended for food, there is certainly no fault in using a new one once; however, there is an offense in reusing them, as explained in the Vinaya.

At the place where the meal is prepared in the donor's house, the ground must be smeared clean with cow dung; small seats must be arranged individually, and clean jars and pots must be prepared in advance to store plenty of water.
Once the monks have arrived, they shall loosen the ties of their robes and set down their water jars; they should then examine the water.
If it is free of insects, they may use it to wash their feet. Thereafter, each shall sit upon a small bench to rest for a short while, observing the time of day.

When the sun was about at its zenith, the donor announced that the time had arrived. The assembly of practitioners then adjusted their upper robes by folding back the two corners and tying them in front; they tucked the right corner of the lower edge under the waistband on the left side. Having cleansed their hands with either ash or earth, they either accepted water offered by the donor or used their own *kuṇḍikā* (water flask) as the occasion required. Resuming their seated posture, they received the vessels and bowls.
Wash briefly with water, taking care not to let it flow across the floor.
Before the meal, there is no ritual of reciting incantations or prayers.

The donor then washes their hands and feet thoroughly and first places the offering for the Holy Sangha before the assembled community; subsequently, they distribute the food to serve the monastic assembly.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the meal distribution, set aside one dish of food to offer to the Mother Hārītī.

In a previous life, this mother had made a vow to eat all the children of Rājagṛha for a certain reason; because of that evil vow, she abandoned her body and was reborn among the yakṣas. She gave birth to five hundred sons, and every day they would devour the boys and girls of Rājagṛha.
The people informed the Buddha, who then hid his young son, named Aññā-Koṇḍañña.
They searched for him everywhere until they found him by the side of the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"Do you cherish your son?
You have five hundred sons, yet you still cherish even one;
how much more so for others, of whom there are but one or two?"
The Buddha, through his transformative power, caused her to receive the five precepts and become an upāsikā.
She then requested of the Buddha,
"What do my five hundred sons eat now?"
The Buddha said:
"In the monasteries where bhikṣus reside, sacrificial food is provided daily to ensure that you have sufficient meals.

Therefore, in the various temples of the Western Regions, an image of a mother holding a child is painted in white on the porch or near the kitchen; beneath her knees, there are either five or three [other children] to represent her likeness.
Every day, she would prepare and present sumptuous offerings of food.
Her mother was among the retinues of the Four Heavenly Kings and possessed great power and majesty.
Those who were ill or childless would offer food to her, and all their wishes were fulfilled.
The extensive details are as found in the Vinaya; this account merely sets forth the general meaning.
This deity existed previously in China, where she was known as Guizimuzi (Kauṣīkī).
Furthermore, in all the great monasteries of the Western Regions, her image is carved in wood beside the pillars of the kitchen or in front of the gates of the main storehouse.
Some are two or three chi in height, fashioned in the likeness of a *śrīdeva* (spirit-king). They sit cradling a golden bag while squatting on a small stool, with one foot hanging down to the ground.
Each is smeared with oil to give it a black appearance; they are called Mahākāla, which means the Great Black Deity.

According to ancient tradition, it is said that he is a subordinate of Mahādeva; by nature, he loves the Triple Gem and protects the fivefold assembly, ensuring they suffer no loss and that the needs of those who seek his aid are fulfilled according to their wishes.
Whenever it was time for the meal, the kitchen staff would invariably offer incense and lamps, and all the food and drink would be set out before them.

I personally witnessed this at the Pāṇḍana Monastery, where they speak of the Great Nirvāṇa; there, the monks usually number over one hundred. However, during the biannual festivals of spring and autumn, when the time for worship arrives, five hundred monks may unexpectedly arrive just as the midday meal is being served. Since it is precisely the hour of noon, it is not permissible to cook further.
The administrator said to the kitchen staff,
"In the midst of such an emergency, what should we do?
At that time, an elderly female attendant spoke to them, saying:
"This is but a routine matter; there is no need for you to worry.
Thereupon, he lit many incense sticks, laid out a bountiful array of sacrificial offerings, and addressed the Black Deity, saying:
"The Great Sage has entered Nirvana, yet his disciples still remain. Monks from the four quarters have arrived to pay homage at the holy traces."
"Providing food and drink without allowing anything to be lacking is the power of your benevolence; you should know that it is time.

He then immediately commanded the entire assembly to sit down, and the monastery’s regular meals were served in order until everyone was fully satisfied; yet the amount of food remaining was exactly as it had been on ordinary days.
Everyone cried out in praise, extolling the power of the celestial deity.
Because they had personally gone to pay their respects and behold the deity’s countenance, they saw that before them, the food had formed into a great mass.
They asked what the meaning of this was.
He reported the circumstances of this:
"Although there were none previously in the region north of the Huai River, there are many places where they are established in the south of the Yangtze.
Those who have sought them have witnessed their efficacy; thus, the Way of the Spirits is not empty."
The practice at Dajue Temple for the Mucilinda Dragon is likewise extraordinary.
Regarding the method of serving food, ginger and salt are presented first.
The ginger consists of one or two pieces, each about the size of a finger, while the salt is a full or half spoonful placed upon leaves.

The one who distributes the salt should kneel with palms joined before the elder and chant "Tri-pātra-khaṭa," which is translated as "well-arrived" (śan-zhì); the old transcription "seng-ba" is erroneous.
The Elder said:
"With the intention of distributing food equally, the provisions for the Path have been well-prepared.
When the time for eating arrived again, it was appropriate that it should be so according to the meaning of those words.

Nevertheless, when the Buddha and the great assembly received that poisoned food, the Buddha instructed them to chant the *triphalakṛta* mantra before eating; consequently, all the poisonous drugs were transformed into delicious flavors.
Speaking from this perspective, these are indeed esoteric expressions; they do not necessarily refer to the arrival of the "Good" (Śānti).

Regarding the two sounds "Xi" and "Shi," one follows whichever is appropriate for the occasion. As for the practice of chanting "Shi" in the regions of Bing and Fen, there are many established precedents.

The person serving the food must stand directly in front with feet together, bowing the body with reverence, and holding the vessel and the cakes or fruit with both hands. The food should be suspended at a distance of one *vitasti* (the span of the thumb and forefinger) from the hand; for other vessels or solid foods, the distance should be one or two *aṅgulas*.
If one were to deviate from this path, the principle would not support such acceptance.
One should accept and eat as it comes, without the trouble of waiting for the food to be distributed to all.
The phrase "waiting until the food is served to everyone" is not the correct translation, nor is the practice of eating at will after the meal has ended a teaching of the Noble Ones.
Next, he was served dry non-glutinous rice and thick bean stew, poured over with hot clarified butter.
He stirred them together with his hand to blend them, added various seasonings, and ate using his right hand.
When the stomach is only half full, one may then partake of cakes and fruits; subsequently, one consumes milk, curd, and granulated sugar.
For drinking, one takes cold water regardless of whether it is winter or summer.
This is the regular diet of the monastic community, and the general procedure for providing offerings during ritual feasts is likewise the same.

However, the intent of this method of *poṣadha* lies in its profound generosity; the remaining cakes and rice overflowed from the plates and bowls, and even the butter and curd spilled across the ground, where everyone partook as they encountered them.

Thus, during the Buddha’s lifetime, when King Prasenajit personally made offerings to the Buddha and the assembly, he distributed the leftover food and butter and curd until they flowed and spread across the earth; that this is recorded in the Vinaya is precisely this very event.
When Jing arrived in the kingdom of Dharmarājika in Eastern India, he wished to live with frugality and provide offerings for the Sangha.
The people of the time stopped him, saying:
"If you merely wish to suffice for your own needs, why would that not be possible?"
However, according to tradition inherited from antiquity, the offerings must be abundant; if they merely suffice to fill one's belly, I fear people might laugh at us.
I have heard that you, Master, come from a great kingdom where provisions are plentiful; if there is no surplus, it would be better not to set out any offerings at all.
Therefore, one should again rely upon those teachings.
This is because when the mind of giving is vast and expansive, the reward obtained will likewise be abundant; there is no contradiction with principle here.
If one is indeed poor, then when distributing alms after a meal, one should act according to one's own capacity.
When the meal is finished, one rinses the mouth with a small amount of water, swallowing it rather than discarding it.
One places a little water in a vessel, briefly cleans the right hand, and only then does one rise.

When intending to rise from the meal, one must take a full handful of food with the right hand and carry it outside; one should not discriminate between items belonging to the Sangha or to private individuals.
The Sage has enjoined that this be universally bestowed upon sentient beings, yet there is no established instruction in the Vinaya for presenting such food before one has eaten.

Furthermore, he took a plate of food and offered it to his deceased ancestors and other spirits and ghosts who were entitled to eat it; this occurred at Vulture Peak, as described in detail in the sutra.
One should place the food before the senior monk (upādhyāya) and kneel; the senior monk then sprinkles a few drops of water and recites this prayer of blessing:
"By the merit cultivated now, May it universally reach those in the realm of hungry ghosts.
Having eaten, may they be freed from extreme suffering, And upon casting off this body, be reborn in a place of bliss."

In discussing killing, it constitutes a full course of action (*karmapatha*) only when one first acts with intentional purpose and severs the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of another;
if it is not done intentionally, the Buddha stated that there is no offense.

The purity of the three bases establishes the absence of transgression; should one deviate from this principle, one merely incurs a minor offense. Because there was no intent to kill, the causal basis for the act is not fully established.
This is just as when receiving other [precepts], the analogy becomes clearly manifest.
Since the reasons and analogies are already clear and beyond reproach, they are self-evident according to our own tenets.

Why trouble oneself further with forced interpretations, thereby causing the "five-day" doubt to emerge from the author's pen and the error of "three boars" (sishi) to be transmitted through the words of those who faithfully accept [the teaching]?
If one personally begs for raw cocoons and observes firsthand that they harm the insects, this is something even a layperson ought not to do, let alone one whose heart aspires to liberation.
To cite this as proof is profoundly untenable.

If there is a donor who brings an offering with a pure intention, one must immediately lead them in joyful appreciation (anumodanā) to accept it; using it to sustain the body and cultivate virtue is truly without fault.
The Dharma robes of the five regions of India may be stitched and sewn as one pleases.

To fulfill the requirements of outward appearance, why rely on anything particularly refined or exquisite?

If one wears the patched robe (*nāṃsi*), the intention lies in simplifying affairs; whether picking up what is discarded from a heap of refuse or taking what is cast away from a cemetery, one sews it as soon as it is obtained, merely to ward off cold and heat.
Yet some have said: "In the Vinaya, 'bedding and requisites' refers to the three robes.

Upon seeing the prohibition against wild silkworms, they conceived a mistaken notion and concluded that dharma-robes must not be made of silk; they then immediately sought out cotton cloth with great diligence.

It would be better to concede that the original text refers to a mat, and that *kauśeya* is simply the name for silkworms; thus, silk produced from them retains this designation. Since its substance is a precious material, the regulations prohibit its use.
There are two methods for making mats:
either one may sew them into a bag and store wool within, or they may be woven from silk, such as the class of *kūṭha* (woolen carpets).
The dimensions of this matting should be two cubits in width and four cubits in length, with its thickness adjusted according to the season.
Begging for it oneself is prohibited, but receiving it as a gift from another incurs no offense.
To use such a mat entirely without permission is a grave violation of the strict regulations.
These various bedding materials are not the three robes (*tricīvara*).
Furthermore, the Vinaya speaks of "right livelihood" (*samyagājīva*), which means that one’s primary concern must be the sustenance of one's body.

According to the Vinaya teachings, when the Sangha cultivates fields, they must share the harvest with pure persons (śuddhapuruṣa) according to a fixed proportion; alternatively, they may do so with other households, with one-sixth being drawn from the total in all cases.
The monastic community is provided only with cattle and land, while they remain entirely ignorant of all other affairs.
It may be appropriate to divide and measure [the resources] according to the time; in most monasteries of the Western Regions, this is generally the case.
Some are greedy and do not divide the harvest into portions, personally employing their slaves and servants to manage the farming themselves; monks who guard the precepts will not eat their food.

Even if one’s daily consumption does not exceed one *śu* (one *lì*), who could possibly withstand the weight of a hundred such transgressions?

Therefore, men of upright integrity loathe the complexity of worldly affairs; carrying their water jars and alms bowls, they abandon them and gallop toward the distant wilderness. Sitting alone in the quiet forests and wilds, they joyfully take birds and deer as their companions, severing the clamor of fame and profit, and cultivating the tranquil extinction of Nirvana.

If one seeks profit for various households through the recitation of scriptures, this is permitted by the Vinaya; however, tilling the soil and harming living beings is not allowed by the Gate of the Teaching.
To damage insects and obstruct one's practice—could there be anything more excessive than this?
Regarding the ten *qǐng* of sinful and heterodox births, when one composes works on them, they do not appear as mere peripheral branches;

Furthermore, he saw a junior monk who sent his young attendant to deliver two *sheng* of rice to the women of his family, an act involving illicit intimacy.
Someone informed the assembly, and the monk was summoned for interrogation.

However, as the community of nuns collectively observes these rules, there is no need for official regulations.
Furthermore, I have observed that when women enter the temple, they do not go into the quarters; instead, they converse together in the corridors and depart after a short while.
Furthermore, he saw within the monastery a bhikṣu named Harivarman, who was then about thirty years of age; his conduct was peerless, and his reputation was far-reaching.
One day he recited the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, which contains seven hundred stanzas.
He was proficient in the three piṭakas of the inner scriptures and thoroughly versed in the four clarities of secular learning; throughout the Eastern Holy Land, he was esteemed as the foremost.
Since receiving full ordination, she had never spoken face-to-face with women; even when her mother or sisters came, she would merely go out to see them.
At that time, they asked her:

He replied:
"My nature is prone to defilement; without this, its source cannot be blocked.
Although it is not something prohibited by the Sages, what harm is there in using it to guard against depravity?
Furthermore, he saw those of great virtue and extensive learning, some of whom had mastered a single *piṭaka* through diligent study.

The community provided them with superior quarters and assigned pure attendants (*śrāmaṇera*) to serve them; they lectured on a regular basis, were exempted from monastic duties, traveled in numerous carriages, and did not even ride on saddled animals.

Furthermore, when seeing a visiting monk newly arrive at the monastery, one provides him with excellent food for five days along with the assembly, hoping to allow him to rest and recover; thereafter, he follows the regular routine of the monks.
If he is a person of good character, the Sangha shall invite him to reside, granting him the credit for his summer retreat and providing him with bedding and requisites.

If he lacks learning, he shall be treated as one of the permanent members of the Sangha; provided he possesses extensive knowledge, he shall be granted the aforementioned status, his name shall be entered into the monastic register, and he shall be considered equal to those who have long resided there.
Furthermore, seeing that he had come with a sincere heart, [the Master] questioned him in detail regarding his reasons.
If he sought to leave the household life, the Sangha would perform the tonsure for him.
His name would not be entered into the royal registers; the Sangha maintains its own internal records.
If, later on, anyone breaks the precepts or acts improperly, they shall be struck with the *gandī* and expelled.
For this reason, the members of the Saṃgha must examine one another, so that the arising of faults and difficulties may be prevented from its very inception.
At that time, he sighed and said:
