Had you not previously taken a step toward the West, how could you have discerned these correct principles!"

This is either a communal regulation of the monastery or a personal vow of essential practice; all other matters are recorded in the Vinaya texts, yet these are of utmost importance for maintaining the Dharma in the final age.
These are all the regulations of the Dhārmarājika-vihāra. As for the Nālandā monastery, its rules are even more stringent;

consequently, it maintains a monastic community of over three thousand members and possesses more than two hundred villages as fiefdoms, all of which were bestowed by successive kings throughout the generations.
To ensure that the flourishing [of the Dharma] remains uninterrupted, how can one discuss matters without adhering to the Vinaya?

Yet, we have not yet seen a secular official sitting in formal session at the yamen while the monastics stand in rows to the side; nor have we seen them treated with such contemptuous summoning as if they were commoners, or subjected to the exhaustion of travel for sending off the old and welcoming the new.
If their oversight is not caught, they rush to the public offices and demand an audience with the clerks, regardless of whether it is winter or summer.

Now, those who have left the household life originally do so because they aspire to transcend the secular world, abandoning the perilous path of the five fears and following the level highway of the Eightfold Noble Path.
How could one instead hasten back toward worldly affairs, once again entangling oneself in the net of suffering? If one seeks simplicity and stillness, how could such a goal ever be realized?
This may be called being entirely contrary to liberation and not conforming to the state of serene detachment.

In principle, one must observe the twelve dhūtas and possess the thirteen requisites; sustaining life according to circumstances to wash away old habits, thereby repaying the great bounty of one's teachers, fellow monks, and parents, and requiting the profound kindness of devas, nāgas, and sovereign rulers.
This is indeed the refined and harmonious ritual for self-mastery and the excellent path for encouraging cultivation.
Having discussed the matter of protecting life, let us further speak of its actual practice.
I pray that the Venerable Ones will not find this prolixity tiresome.
Regarding the distinctions among the four schools, they manifest their differences through the manner of wearing the lower robe (*nivasana*):
in the Sarvāstivāda school, both sides are folded outward in a double pleat.

The Mahāsāṃghikas fold the right hem of their lower garment toward the left, tucking it inward so that it does not fall; the manner of wearing the skirt by Western women is no different from that of the Mahāsāṃghikas.
The Sarvāstivādins and Saṃmitīyas follow the same method of construction, differing only in that they turn the hem outward and tuck it straight across to the side.
The construction of waistbands is likewise different; for nuns, they follow the divisions as for monks, with no distinct form at all.

Furthermore, in the land of China, items such as the *cīvara*, the *ekāṃśa*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, the square skirt, the *kaṣāya* trousers, and the long robe and tunic all deviate from their original design—not only do they share sleeves and connected seams, but they differ entirely from the authentic style.
As for wearing robes that do not conform to the Vinaya regulations, one incurs an offense for every item used.
There are even those who travel as far as the Western Regions (India) only to be ridiculed by all; filled with shame and inner remorse, they tear their robes to use them for miscellaneous purposes.
These are all garments that do not conform to the Dharma.
If I remain silent and do not speak, those who know will have no way to understand;
yet if I wish to speak directly, I fear those who hear me may resent me.

For this reason, I have deliberated deeply within my limited thoughts and hesitated over whether to proceed or retreat; I pray that the wise will examine in detail the fundamental protocols regarding clothing.

Furthermore, as for the attire worn by the common people, officials, and the nobility of the Western regions, they possess nothing more than a pair of white cotton garments (*kārpāsa*), while those of the poor and lowly have but a single piece of coarse cloth.
The monastic community of the renunciant dharma maintains only the three robes and six articles; it is only those who delight in abundance, such as wealthy elders, who employ the thirteen requisites.

As for the prohibition against sleeves and connected back-seams in the land of the Eastern Xia, this is merely a case of those practicing in the eastern regions speaking recklessly about the Western Kingdom.
To speak briefly of the people and their clothing in Jambudvīpa and its surrounding seas:
from Mahābodhi to the city of Lin-yi to the east, there are more than twenty kingdoms, which correspond precisely to the southern borders of Huān Prefecture.

To the southwest, reaching the sea to the north, including Kashmir and the various countries of the southern seas—numbering more than ten—as well as the island of Siṃhala, all of these wear the two *kaṣāyas*.
Having neither waistbands nor tailoring, they simply wrap two *xun* of wide cloth around the waist and tuck it underneath.
Beyond the Western Heavens, on the coastal frontiers of the great ocean, there are the countries of Persia (*Bālāsī*) and Tāḍi, where people wear both shirts and trousers.
In the Land of the Naked (Nagnāṭaka), there are no clothes at all; both men and women are entirely bare-bodied.

From Kaśmīra onwards, including the various Hu peoples such as the Suli, Tibetans, and Turks, the general customs are similar: they do not wear garments made of *kambala* (cotton cloth), but instead prioritize felt and fur, with very little *kārpāsa* (cotton).
As for those who maintain [the practice] at present, because it is a cold land, wearing shirts and trousers is the norm.
Among these various countries, only Persia, the Land of the Naked, Tibet, and the Turks have never had the Buddha-dharma; all others revere and uphold it.

Furthermore, in regions where people wear shirts and trousers, none practice washing for purification; it is for this reason that the land of the Five Indias prides itself on its purity and loftiness.

Yet, as for refined elegance, scholarly grace, the observance of etiquette, the richness of their food, and the abundance of benevolence and righteousness—these qualities belong uniquely to the Eastern Land (China), and none can surpass it. It is only in matters such as not observing dietary purity, not washing after using the toilet, and not chewing *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks) that these practices differ from those of the Western Regions.

As for the claim that there is no fault in currently wearing non-Dharmic clothing, citing the passage from the *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* which states, "What is impure in this region may be pure in another region; thus one may practice it without transgression," this is merely an error of the translator; the intended meaning is not so.
This is as detailed elsewhere.
If that is so, then for *bhikṣus* in China, anything other than the three robes is not in accordance with the noble tradition.

Since such items would constitute an offense and are logically unfit for use, consider, for instance, the warm lands of the West, where a single cotton cloth is sufficient to sustain one throughout the entire year.
As for those wishing to depart for the cold lands beyond the Snowy Ranges, how can they ensure their survival, physical well-being, and progress in their vocations?
The Sage’s sincere words state that "to mortify the body and toil with diligence" is the teaching of external paths.
As for the principle of what to adopt and what to reject, what could one possibly desire?

However, since the sages established and disseminated the practice of wearing clothing so that it might reach even cold regions, this is sufficient to nourish the body; how, then, could it ever hinder the Way?
In Sanskrit, it is called *lipa*, which is translated as "the garment that wraps the belly.

To briefly describe its form and construction: one removes the front and back panels and takes only the side-draped portion; one side must not have sleeves, and it should consist of a single width of cloth just sufficient to pass through the arms.

The shoulder straps should not be wide; they are worn on the left side and must not be overly broad. On the right side, the straps cross over so that wind cannot penetrate; they should be lined with plenty of cotton wool and made thick and warm.
There is also a style where the right side is sewn closed with a button-hole at the armpit for threading the head through; this is its original construction.
Observing firsthand the Western regions, I have often seen monks from the Hu lands carrying such garments;
yet, this attire is not seen at Nālandā, for it is simply because the country is hot and its people do not use it.

Based on this intended meaning, it is specifically for the elderly in cold regions that the practice of baring the right shoulder while keeping the back covered was established; there is no precedent for following this by adding the exposure of the right side, which violates fundamental decorum. Such a fabrication constitutes a deliberate transgression of the Dharma.
As for standing, walking, or hugging one’s belly, these serve to protect oneself from severe cold;
wearing thick robes as an outer layer is sufficient to shield against intense freezing.
In places where images are located, when performing prostrations before the Honored One, it is customary to expose the shoulders; to cover them would incur an offense.

That being so, those who have left the household life to simplify their affairs may reside in their rooms during the winter months with charcoal fires as the season requires; why then should they trouble themselves to wear many garments?
If there is a medical necessity that makes wearing them essential, one should decide on the matter according to the circumstances at the time, ensuring that it does not violate the proper decorum.
However, in the Eastern Land (China), the cold is so severe that it splits the body; if one does not wear warm clothing, people will inevitably suffer from emaciation and death.
Since these are such difficult conditions, it is logically necessary to provide widespread relief.

The square skirt and the *ekāṃśa* (one-shoulder) style are simple and distinct from worldly fashions; the *pāṭa* robe is worn only during the depths of winter as a temporary concession for those whose lives would otherwise be endangered by the cold, knowing it is not the original design and thus feeling deep shame, like oil placed upon a cart.
If one can truly refrain from wearing them, that is an excellent matter.
As for other items such as robes, trousers, leggings, and shirts, all must be strictly prohibited.
Once the severe cold has passed, it is improper to wear these upon the body; furthermore, to again wear a vest (pianshan) is certainly not permitted.
This, then, is to discard the superfluous and grasp the essential, looking upward to accord with the Sage’s intent.
While it may be permissible for oneself to fall [into error] once, to transmit such [errors] to others would surely mislead the masses.
If one can abandon this old path and strive to follow a new course, then one may truly be said to continue the lineage of Shaoshi, building a bridge to Vulture Peak so that both stand equally lofty.
The royal city of Rājagṛha was leveled, its imperial precincts encompassed as one;
the great Yellow River merged its waters with the literary pond, and the slender willows shared their radiance with the Bodhi tree.
As the mulberry fields were transformed and flourished anew, they cast forth their brilliance throughout the duration of the kalpa-stone.
Truly lamentable! Truly a matter for diligent endeavor!

Yet, since the Sun of the Buddha has already set and the Teaching remains only in this later age, to practice it is to face the Great Master in person, while to turn one's back on the Teaching is to have all transgressions manifest before one.
Therefore, a sutra says: "If one can uphold the precepts, then my presence is no different from now.
Others may say:
"The virtuous elders of old all remained silent; why should people today change their standards for the sake of later generations?"
This is certainly not the case.

According to the Dharma, there are extensive teachings regarding those who are not [ordinary] persons; examining the Vinaya Piṭaka, one may accept food and clothing only when they are free from fault.
"It is not the knowing that is difficult; it is the practicing that is hard.
If one hears but does not practice, can the guide be said to have erred?
He spoke again:
For all classes of sentient beings, food and clothing are their primary concerns; these serve as shackles that bind them to the field of birth.
To follow the words of the Sage is to transcend existence with serene detachment; to indulge one's own whims is to be dragged along by the accumulation of transgressions.
The wise must discern this, for the matter lies before them.
Like a jewel resting in mud, or water dwelling within a lotus, once one is free from the eight winds, how could the five fears ever entangle them?
With robes that barely cover the body and food that merely sustains life, he is dedicated solely to seeking liberation, having no desire for the realms of humans or devas.

He shall spend his life in the practice of *dhūta* austerities and devote his years to saving sentient beings; casting aside the falsehoods of the nine gates, he aspires to the perfect solidity of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Thus, he is worthy of receiving offerings from five hundred [disciples] and bringing merit and benefit to three thousand [beings].
11. The Method for Wearing Robes (11). Regarding the method for wearing the three robes (*tricīvara*) and the fashioning of their ties and fasteners, these are set forth according to the Vinaya.

One may take a robe measuring five *cubits* and fold it into three pleats. At the point where the shoulder is folded, one should place a square patch, four or five finger-widths from the edge, with the patch itself being five finger-widths square.
The four sides of the collar are stitched, and a small hole is pierced through the center with an awl to secure the collar-fastener (*kṣepa*).

This fastener may be made of cord or silk; its thickness should be similar to that of a shirt-fastener, approximately two finger-widths in length, tied into a "concentric" knot, while the remainder is cut off.
Pierce holes in the lapels and pull them outward, fastening them crosswise to form two lapels; then, tie a knot within this central space.
As for the edges of the overlapping section at the chest, attach buttons just as one would for the buttons on a shirt.
This is precisely that method.
First, I have presented the original composition according to its general outline; however, if one wishes to master the subtle essence of this method, it must ultimately be transmitted face-to-face.
As for the fastening loops and buttons at the lower edge of the robe, they may be applied as desired for wearing; this was permitted by the Sage.
At both ends, about eight finger-widths from the corners, attach one toggle and one button each; these are required for the time of eating.
Fold the edges back over the chest so that the buttons meet; this constitutes the essential point.

Whenever one is within the monastery or in the presence of the assembly, one must never wear the robe with fasteners or with the shoulders covered by a cowl; however, when traveling outside or entering lay dwellings, it is necessary to fasten the ties, while at other times one may simply drape the robe over the shoulders.

When attending to private affairs in seclusion, one may adjust the robe as desired; however, when in the presence of a venerable image, it must be kept neat and orderly. One should drape the wide corner of the right sleeve over the left shoulder and let it hang behind the back, rather than placing it upon the elbow.
If one wishes to wear it with a fastening loop, one must first drape it over both shoulders, then tuck the loop inside and direct it toward the back of the shoulders so that it does not slip off.

With the corner of the robe resting on the shoulder, the garment is then wrapped around the neck; both hands emerge from below, and one corner extends forward—this is precisely the style of the image of King Aśoka.
When going out, holding a parasol is a graceful and dignified manner of conduct; this is precisely following the instructions to wear the upper robe in a neat and orderly fashion.
The parasol may be woven from bamboo; it need only be as thin as a single layer of a bamboo mat, and its size may be adjusted as desired to two or three feet in width.

A second layer should be made at the top to serve as a handle; the length of this handle should be measured according to the width of the canopy. It may be fashioned by thinly coating it with lacquer, or woven from *mālu* grass, or like a wicker hat; even by sandwiching paper between layers, it will become sturdy.

Although this practice was not previously prevalent in China, its adoption is nonetheless essential; for when there is a torrential rain, it prevents one's clothes from becoming soaked, and when there is scorching heat, it truly brings forth a sense of coolness.
Since it accords with the Vinaya to benefit the body, carrying it [the bowl] is certainly not harmful.
Regarding the essential matters discussed here, most are not practiced in China.

When the corner of the *kāṣāya* hangs down, it should properly resemble an elephant’s trunk; even when Indian monks arrive, they all follow this convention. This is truly because the silk is so smooth that it slips off the shoulder, which has caused the correct rule to fall into disuse and corruption.

Later, when the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty arrived and transmitted the method of "shoulder-draping," many ancient worthies still expressed their disapproval; those who cling to antiquity and remain deluded are found everywhere.
Regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*): if one installs short ties and cuts the long cords, the transgression of violating the teachings is immediately avoided;
if one wears the *saṃkakṣikā* (cross-shoulder robe) and removes the waist border, the labor of needle and thread is simultaneously ceased.

All flasks and alms bowls should be suspended from both shoulders; as soon as they reach the armpits, they must not be crossed over. Their straps should not be too long, being sufficient only to pass over the shoulders; if they cross at the chest, it will cause one’s breath to become labored.
If something was not originally part of the formal practice, it simply cannot be implemented.
Regarding the ritual for the alms-bowl bag (*pātraka*), it shall be explained below.
In the northern regions of Sūli, many people commonly use cross-straps; however, such regional adaptations are certainly not the Buddha’s original injunction.

If there is another robe, one should first drape it over the shoulder and then generally wear it to cover the outer robe and bowl. Whether proceeding toward a monastery or visiting a layperson's home, one must reach the quarters to set down the umbrella before finally untying the knots and hanging up the robe and bowl.
Place many ivory objects on the wall in front of the room so that there will be no lack of space for items to be set out at the last moment.
The rest is the same as explained in the twenty-sixth chapter, "On Meeting Guests."
However, those who make their *kāṣāya* from thin silk find it mostly too slippery; it refuses to stay on the shoulder, and during prostrations, it consequently falls to the ground.
One should choose materials that do not slip off, such as *śī* (silk gauze), *chou* (raw silk), or white cotton cloth (*pata*), which are essential for this purpose.
The *saṃkakṣikā* garment is for covering the shoulders; it becomes compliant with the original regulations only when an additional cubit is added.
As for the method of wearing it, one should expose the right shoulder and cross it over the left shoulder; it should be worn constantly within the dwelling quarters.
Only this [robe] and the lower garment (*śīrṣaka*) are required; when going out to pay respects to the Honored One, one may add other garments as appropriate.
Regarding the method for wearing the lower garment, I shall briefly set forth its general outline.
As for the style of the lower garment according to the Sarvāstivāda school: it is five cubits in width and two cubits in length, made of silk, fine cloth, or cotton as available.
In the Western lands, these [robes] are all made as single layers, whereas in the land of China (Shenzhou), they are made double-layered according to preference.

They may be arranged horizontally or vertically as one desires; once the wrapping around the body is complete, lift them so that they pass above the navel, then with the right hand, pull the upper corner on the left side inward toward the right side of the waist.

Take the outer edge of the lower garment on the left side and cover the left flank; that which is near the right hand is the right fold (*yòuqú*), and that which is near the left hand is the left fold (*zuǒqú*). Raise both hands at the two sides to make them even and level; when the center is held upright and straight, three pleats (*sānjié*) will be formed.

Afterward, contract both hands individually toward the waist and fold all three layers together to cover them behind; lift each corner by three fingers and insert them toward the spine, allowing them to descend about three finger-widths into the waist.
Thus, even if one has not yet tied the sash, it will remain fastened to the body without falling.

Afterwards, taking the waist sash—approximately five cubits in length—one hooks it at its center and lifts it toward the area below the navel. One then folds the upper edge of the skirt backward into two rows, crosses them over in front, and pulls them out to the left and right. Holding both sides firmly with one hand for each, one wraps the two strands around three times; if there is excess, it should be cut off, and if there is too little, more should be added.

12. The Twelve Rules for the Funeral Attire of Bhikṣuṇīs. Regarding the funeral attire of bhikṣuṇīs in the lands of the Eastern Continent (China), their robes all conform to worldly customs; most of what they wear and use deviates from the proper ritual protocol.

As for the method of tying the sash, the measurement is the same as that for the *saṃghāṭī*.

The area between the chest and the armpits is entirely devoid of any binding or fastening; whether one is in the prime of youth or in declining years, the fact that the breasts rise and the flesh bulges is truly beyond reproach.

At the moment of death, sins fall like a drizzling rain; even if ten thousand people were to try, would there be but one who could still reform?

However, when going outside, in the presence of the Sangha, or when accepting an invitation for a meal at a layperson's home, one must wrap the *kāṣāya* around the neck to cover the body; it is improper to loosen the shoulder-fasteners, nor should one expose the chest while reaching down with the hands to eat.

Within the rooms of that monastery, both the *kusulaka* and the *saṃkakṣikā* are sufficient; according to a consultation of the Sanskrit original, there is no specific name for a "shoulder-covering robe," which refers precisely to the *saṃkakṣikā* garment.
This is the original designation for the *saṃkakṣikā*; since it is not referred to as a "skirt," there must have been discrepancies in the transmission and translation.

Sincere in heart and possessing few desires, he devoted himself to the true path of secluded tranquility.

By distancing oneself from worldly affairs and reducing the number of disciples, one is like a gem buried in mud or a lotus in water; though called a member of the lower assembly, in actual wisdom one is equal to those of the upper ranks.

In all such cases, one may use the mind-seal to designate this location.
Within this monastery, or perhaps in a single room,

Regarding the "one who maintains the dharma," this refers to the one who maintains the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) to establish the boundary, as described in the *Ekottara-karman*.

For example, if the boundary for robes has not yet been established, staying apart [from one's robes] incurs an offense;

The same applies to the pure kitchen.

Furthermore, regarding the method for protecting robes, although the boundaries may differ—such as those defined by trees and so forth—one merely protects the demarcated area; the intention is certainly not to prevent contact with women.
If a *karmadāna* enters the kitchen, how could he be considered a "village collector"?

For the *karmadāna* to hold the robes and inspect them is merely an excessive and hasty measure.

14. The Fivefold Community’s Rains Retreat (Varṣā). 15. Regarding the Fivefold Community’s Rains Retreat: if it is the earlier retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*), it begins on the first day of the dark fortnight of the fifth month;
if it is the later retreat (*paścimavarṣā*), it begins on the first day of the dark fortnight of the sixth month.
Only on these two days may one enter the *varṣā* retreat together; there is no scriptural authorization for doing so in the interval between them.

When the fifteenth day of the eighth month arrives, the earlier summer retreat is concluded; when the fifteenth day of the ninth month arrives, the later summer retreat is concluded. At these times, both the monastic community and the laity vigorously engage in making offerings.
From the middle of the eighth month onward, it is called the month of Kārttika; in Jiangnan, the Kaṭhina ceremony is held precisely at this time, when the preceding summer retreat has concluded.
The sixteenth day of the eighth month is the day for spreading the kaṭhina robe; this is the ancient rule.

Furthermore, the Vinaya text states: "Whenever one is within the summer retreat and has a legitimate reason requiring the acceptance of [extra] days, regardless of how many such reasons arise, one must immediately accept them in accordance with those days."
When the matter of a single night's stay arose, he accepted it for one day;
in this manner, it continued up to seven days, each time with a different person.
When further circumstances arose, the Vinaya prescribed that he should go after being formally invited again.

If one has already passed seven days and it is now the eighth day or beyond, up until the forty-night period, one may receive the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for staying away for eight days or more; however, one must not stay abroad for longer than half a summer retreat. For this reason, only a forty-night period is permitted.
If one must go elsewhere due to illness or various difficulties, even if one does not formally receive the [remaining] days of the retreat, the *anvāsaṃvāsa* (summer retreat) is not broken.
Once the five groups of the ordained have entered the *anvāsaṃvāsa*, those of lower status who have business may depart after having entrusted their affairs to others.
Before the summer retreat begins, rooms are pre-allocated; the senior monk takes the best one, and they are distributed in order until everyone has been assigned.
This practice is currently observed at Nālandā Monastery, where the community distributes rooms every year.
The World-Honored One’s direct instruction is profoundly beneficial:

first, it eliminates the grasping at a self; second, it provides universal protection for the monastic quarters. It is indeed appropriate that those who have left the household life should perform this practice.
However, as for the occasional division of monasteries in the region south of the Yangtze River, this was handed down by the virtuous masters of old and its practice is still maintained today.
How could one allow oneself to occupy a single courtyard and claim it as one's own property, failing to consider whether such an arrangement is appropriate until the end of one's life?
This is truly because it was not practiced by those of former generations, which has caused later people to lose the Dharma.
If one were able to divide [the retreat] according to the teachings, there would indeed be profound benefit.

15. Rules for the *Pravāraṇā* (The End of the Summer Retreat). Regarding the rules for the *Pravāraṇā*: at the conclusion of the summer retreat at the end of the year, this day should be called *Pravāraṇā*. This means the sense of "following others" in that, among three matters, one may freely raise issues and confess transgressions to eliminate faults.
The ancient term "self-indulgence" (*pravāraṇā*) is a literal translation of the meaning.

On the night of the fourteenth day, one must invite a master of the scriptures to ascend the high seat and recite the Buddha’s sutras; at that time, laypeople flock like clouds and monastics gather like mist, lighting lamps to provide continuous illumination and making offerings of incense and flowers.

At dawn, they all set out to circumambulate the villages and cities, each with a devout heart worshipping the *caityas*. Carriages and palanquins bearing the sacred images fill the sky with the sound of drums and music; banners and canopies, draped and fluttering, obscure the sun. This is called *samāja*, translated as "harmonious assembly," and it occurs on all days of great fasting.

This is the ritual for the "Walking City" (Cakravartin) practiced in the Divine Land (China). Beginning at the *yuzhong* hour, they return to the monastery; it is not until noon that the great vegetarian feast (*mahā-prāśana*) is held.

After noon, everyone assembles, each taking about a handful of fresh *mārga* grass. Holding it in their hands and treading upon it with their feet, they perform the *yathāsukham* (as one pleases) rite: first the *bhikṣus*, then the *bhikṣuṇīs*, followed by the three lower assemblies.

If the assembly is large and there is fear that the procedure will be protracted, many individuals should be appointed to receive the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) separately. Should anyone be accused of an offense during this time, the matter shall be addressed and cleared according to the Dharma.
At this juncture, whether it be laypeople offering gifts or the Saṃgha itself acting, all items offered shall be brought before the assembly.
The one possessing the five virtues should ask the presiding elder:
"May these items be used as objects for the *svairakārya* (distribution of goods) for the community of monks?
The presiding elder replies:
"It is permitted.
All items such as clothing, knives, needles, and awls, once received, are to be divided equally; this is the teaching.
The reason for offering knives and needles on this day is that one seeks through them wisdom and sharp intelligence.

Once the *caitya-vandana* (veneration of the shrine) has been completed, you may go your separate ways as you please; this signifies that the summer retreat (*varṣā*) has already concluded, so there is no need to remain for another night.
As detailed elsewhere, this will not be explained in full here.

Regarding the confession of offenses: the intention is to set forth one's transgressions and speak of one’s own prior faults, reforming the past and cultivating the future with sincere and earnest self-reproach.

What was formerly called "confession" (sāṃghāti) does not pertain to the disclosure of offenses.

Examining this closely, translating *ksamā* as "repentance" (*zhuīhuì*) seems to lack a traditional basis.

Among the people of the Western Regions, whenever there is a slight error or when individuals physically touch one another, regardless of their seniority, the elder extends his hand toward the other, while the junior joins his palms in reverent submission.

yet, fearing lingering obstructions in the future and seeking to dispel former delusions, although long-established customs may be followed, matters must ultimately rely upon the fundamental principle.

Knowing the Proper Time for Rites. Regarding the method of ritual reverence, it must accord with the prescribed forms; if one does not follow the teachings, one will stumble and fall even on level ground.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"There are two kinds of defiled touch; one should neither receive prostrations nor prostrate to others.
If one violates this instruction, every prostration performed will incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
What are the two defilements?

First is the defilement of food and drink. This means that if one has consumed any substance whatsoever, down to swallowing or chewing a single piece of medicine, until one has rinsed one's mouth and washed one's hands, it is not permissible to receive prostrations from others or to prostrate to others.

If one drinks a beverage, water, or even tea, honey, and other decoctions, as well as ghee or sugar products, and fails to rinse the mouth and wash the hands, the offense is the same as previously described.
The second is impurity through defilement: this refers to when one has not yet washed the body after voiding excrement or urine, nor has one yet washed the hands or rinsed the mouth;

Furthermore, during a communal gathering or a vegetarian feast, joining one's palms is itself an act of reverence; therefore, it is unnecessary to perform a full prostration, as doing so would contravene the teachings.
Whether in a crowded place, on impure ground, or upon a road, performing prostrations constitutes an offense in each case.

Although there are scriptural texts (*vinaya*) for all such matters, because they have been handed down for a long time and because we dwell in a cold country, it is difficult to practice in accordance with the teachings; thus, everyone cites many similar precedents to comfort themselves, and who would ever be willing to pay close attention to minor offenses?
18. Eighteen Matters of Convenience: A Brief Outline of the Rituals for the Use of the Toilet As for the matters of convenience regarding the toilet, the ritual is briefly set forth as follows:

First, put on the bathing skirt (*snānaśāṭī*) and drape the *saṃkakṣikā* over the shoulders. Next, take the water flask (*spraśanaghaṭa*), fill it with water, and carry it up to the toilet. Close the door and shield your body.
One should prepare twenty-seven lumps of earth and place them outside the latrine upon bricks, stones, or small wooden planks.
The dimensions of these bricks or planks should be one cubit in length and half a cubit in width.
Crush that soil into powder and arrange it in two rows, gathering each portion separately.
Place one more lump there, and then take three balls into the latrine and set them aside: one for wiping the body and one for washing the body.
Regarding the method for washing the body: one must first wash the left hand with water and then cleanse it with earth.
There remains one coarse lump; for now, wash the left hand once more with it.
If there are wooden tally-sticks (*śalākā*), it is also good to bring them inside; once they have been used, they must be thrown outside the toilet.
If one must use old paper, it may be discarded within the toilet.

Having finished washing and cleansing, one should then pull down one's garment with the right hand, place the water jar to one side, push open the side door with the right hand, and finally exit carrying the jar in the right hand.
Alternatively, one may embrace the flask with the left arm, clenching the left hand, and use the right hand to close the door before departing.
One should squat on one side at that spot; if a seat is required, one should measure the space accordingly at the appropriate time.

Place the water jar upon your left thigh and press it down with your left arm. First, take seven clods of earth close to your body and wash your left hand with each one individually; afterwards, use the remaining seven clods, washing both hands with each one, ensuring that the brick or wooden surface is thoroughly cleansed.
One pill remains; use it to wash the vessel, then wash your arms, calves, and feet until they are all clean. Afterward, depart as you please.
The water from this vessel is not fit to enter the mouth or touch the lips.
Returning to the room, rinse the mouth with water from the pure flask (*śuci-ghaṭa*).
If one has touched this flask during that business, one must again wash the hands and rinse the mouth before handling other utensils.
This is the ritual for defecation; such is the brief explanation.
If one wishes to simplify the procedure, one may act according to one's own convenience;

The Ritual for Receiving the Precepts: Regarding the monastic procedures for renunciation in the Western lands (India), all are fully possessed of the noble regulations as detailed extensively in the *Ekottara-karman* (The Hundred and One Karmas). This [text] merely provides a brief indication of their general principles.

Those who have resolved to leave the household life should go to a teacher according to their own preference and state their original intention; the teacher shall then skillfully inquire about difficult matters, such as whether they have harmed their parents and so forth.
Once difficulties have ceased, one may grant permission for formal acceptance (*parigraha*).
Having accepted them, one allows them to rest and recover for perhaps ten days or a month; the preceptor then confers upon them the five precepts (*śikṣāpada*), whereby they are called an *upāsaka*.
Prior to this, one does not yet belong to the number of the seven assemblies;
this is the foundation for first entering the Buddha-dharma.

The Master then prepares for him the *kaṣāya*, the *saṃkakṣikā*, the lower robe (*antarvāsaka*), and so forth, as well as the alms bowl and water filter, before formally announcing the matter of his renunciation to the Saṃgha.
Once the monastic community has granted permission, one should request an ācārya.
In a private place, have a barber shave the hair and beard; then, having ensured the temperature is neither too cold nor too hot, instruct him to bathe.

The preceptor then puts on the lower robe for him, skillfully examining whether he is not a eunuch or otherwise disqualified; next, he gives him the upper robe, which the candidate receives by placing it upon his head.
Once the dharma robes have been donned, the preceptor bestows the alms bowl; this is called "leaving home" (pravrajyā).
Next, before his preceptor, the ācārya confers the ten precepts; these may be recited from memory or read from the text.
Once the ordination has been received, he is called a śrāmaṇera, translated as "seeker of tranquility," meaning one who desires to seek the state of parinirvāṇa, the perfect stillness.
The old term *śrāmaṇera* is a truncated and phonetically corrupted rendering;

its translation as "resting in compassion" (*xi ci*) is conceptually plausible but lacks textual authority. In terms of dignified deportment, ritual protocols, requesting instruction, and formal announcements, there is no difference in substance between a *śrāmaṇera* and one who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), provided that they remain free from transgressions regarding the twelve categories of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
There are twelve minor variations regarding the *śikṣamāṇā* (probationary nun).

What are these twelve? First, not distinguishing between robes; second, staying overnight apart from one's robes; third, touching fire; fourth, eating after having finished a meal; fifth, harming living seeds; sixth, discarding impurities upon green grass; seventh, climbing high trees at will; eighth, touching precious objects; ninth, eating leftover or stored food; tenth, damaging the ground; eleventh, not receiving food [properly]; and twelfth, destroying living sprouts.
Regarding these twelve [rules], the two minor ones do not constitute an offense.
For a female trainee (*śikṣamāṇā*), however, she commits an offense after the fifth [rule].
From this point downward, all three assemblies (*saṃgha*) are uniformly required to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*).
Regarding these six dharmas and six secondary dharmas, they are as explained in other places.
Only one who can act in this manner truly fulfills the requirements of the Dharma; such a person is included within the five assemblies and is worthy of receiving offerings and profits.
How could it be that after one has left the household life, the preceptor does not confer the ten precepts? I fear that he might violate the major precepts and fail to achieve his goal.
This would be to falsely bear the name of a *śrāmaṇera* and vainly embrace the title of a renunciant; for the sake of a meager benefit, how can one know that such great harm will result!

As for the statement in the Sūtra that "one is included within the ranks of the Saṃgha even though one has not yet received the ten precepts," this is merely a provisional concession made for a single occasion; how could it be taken as a permanent rule?
Furthermore, in the land of China (Shenzhou), those who leave the household life do so through official ordination; once they have received the tonsure, they provisionally rely upon a single teacher.
The preceptor originally did not inquire about their single obstacle, and the disciple likewise never requested the ten precepts.

Having indulged in the commission of transgressions at will prior to full ordination, when the day for receiving the full precepts arrives, they are made to enter the ritual arena; since the rules of discipline were never taught beforehand, how could they possibly be disciplined and compliant at such a late stage?
The way of the abbot is certainly not thus.
Since it is not permissible to consume [the offerings], how can one doubt that the monastery accepts the gift as a debt?
In principle, one should provide for liberation in accordance with the teachings.

All who seek the Master’s guidance must first request a preceptor; the preceptor shall first inquire about their difficulties, and if they are pure, he shall confer the five precepts upon them. Subsequently, observing their suitability for tonsure, he shall provide them with the *man-tiao* robe and cause them to receive the ten precepts.

Once he is proficient in the ritual procedures and his age requirement is fulfilled, and he desires to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), the preceptor shall examine his resolve; if he is capable of upholding the precepts, the preceptor may then provide him with the six requisites and invite the other nine persons. Whether they enter a small altar (*kṣudramandala*), reside within a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), or within a natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*), they are all permitted to perform the ritual.

Within the ritual precinct, one may either use mats and cushions provided by various households or each person may bring their own seating materials; it suffices to prepare incense and flowers, as elaborate expenditure is unnecessary.

As for those receiving the precepts, they are instructed to perform a prostration to each member of the Sangha three times; alternatively, they may approach and grasp the feet with both hands. Both of these are ritual protocols for reverent salutation according to the sacred teachings.
Once the rites have been performed, he is instructed to request the precepts.
After the three requests have been made, the Preceptor, before the assembly, accepts the robe and bowl for him.
The bowl must be carried on a procession to be presented to the entire assembly; if it conforms to the proper standard, everyone in the assembly will exclaim, "A fine bowl!"
If one does not speak thus, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
Thereafter, one should receive [the precepts] according to the Dharma.
Whether the *karmavācanā* master reads from the text or recites it from memory, both are the sacred teaching.
Once the precepts have been received, one is called an *upasaṃpanna*. Here, *upa* means "near" (*upaniṣad*) and *saṃpanna* means "perfected" (*pariniṣpanna*), referring to *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, receiving the full ordination now is precisely to draw near to *nirvāṇa*.

The former term "fully endowed" (具足) refers to its general meaning. However, once the *karmavācanā* is completed, one must immediately measure the shadow to record the distinctions between the five periods of the day.

As for the method of measuring the shadow: first, take a wooden stick about the length of a small chopstick and one cubit (*hasta*) long; bend one end so that it stands four finger-widths high in the shape of a carpenter’s square, ensuring the two parts do not separate. Place this upright in the sunlight, while laying the remainder of the stick flat on the ground. When the upright shadow aligns with the horizontal stick, then measure the horizontal shadow using those same four finger-widths. A full four finger-widths is called one *pauruṣa*; this continues through many *pauruṣas*, or perhaps one *pauruṣa* plus one or half a finger-width, or even just a single finger-width.
Such additions and subtractions may be inferred by one’s own judgment. As for the term *puruṣa*, it is translated as "person.

The reason a shadow of four finger-breadths is called "one person" is that when a staff is held upright at four finger-breadths and the shadow is likewise four finger-breadths long, if this person stands in the middle, the measure of the shadow is similar to the measure of the body; thus, eight finger-breadths correspond to the two shadows being equal to the measure of the body.
This refers to people of average capacity; it may not necessarily apply to all.
Other matters, whether long or short, may be judged by this standard.
However, one must specify whether [the action] occurs before or after a meal.

Regarding the "five periods," since regional customs differ and the calculation of months varies between inclusive and exclusive systems, it is difficult to understand them in detail unless one points directly to the specific facts.
The first is the winter season, which consists of four months, from the sixteenth day of the ninth month to the fifteenth day of the first month.
The second is the spring season, which also consists of four months, from the sixteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month.
The third is the rainy season, which lasts for only one month, from the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the sixth month.
The fourth refers to the period at the end, lasting for only one day and night, namely the day and night of the sixteenth day of the sixth month.

This is a regulation established by the Buddha specifically within the Vinaya teachings; thus, there is an intentional meaning (*abhiprāya*) clearly expressed in this sequential order.

Next, the Preceptor himself points to the *Prātimokṣa* text to ensure that the participants recognize the characteristics of transgressions before instructing them in the recitation of the precepts.

In all correspondence, whether sending or receiving letters, one should write: "The *śrāmaṇera* [Name]," "The junior *bhikṣu* [Name]," or "The *bhikṣu* of established rank [Name].

This practice does not exist in the West.

Since there is both self-benefit and the benefit of others, maintaining [a bowl] is not a detriment; it must be the single alms-bowl of a dhūta practitioner, for which reason it is not laborious.

20. Bathing According to the Seasons: Regarding the method of bathing, the West differs from the East; however, it is simply that the seasonal adjustments differ slightly from other regions.
Throughout the twelve months, flowers and fruits are always present; they know neither ice nor snow, though there is a slight trace of frost. Although it is often hot, it is not an oppressive heat.

When it is hot, their bodies are free from perspiration; when it is cold, their feet do not crack. Because of this, people frequently bathe and wash, yet their bodies remain pure and clean; every day, they do not eat until they have first bathed.
Furthermore, wherever one goes, there is an abundance of ponds; at that time, the people all considered digging ponds to be a meritorious act.
If one travels for the distance of a single *yi*, twenty or thirty such ponds can be seen in the distance, each measuring perhaps one *mu* or five *mu* in width.
Along its four sides, tāla trees were planted, reaching heights of forty to fifty feet.
The ponds were all fed by rainwater and were as clear and still as a pure river.
At each of the eight caityas, there was a bathing pool for the World-Honored One; their water was exceptionally clear and delicious, differing from that of the others.

The Nālandā Monastery had more than ten large ponds; whenever morning arrived, the monastery would strike the *khaṇḍī* drum to summon the monks to bathe. Each person would carry their own bathing cloth, and whether by the hundreds or by the thousands, they would all go outside the monastery together, dispersing toward the various ponds to perform their ablutions.

As for the method for the bathing robe (*snāna-śāṭī*): take a piece of folded cloth five cubits long and one and a half cubits wide, wrap it around the body so that it encircles it completely, and pull out the old robe. Turn both ends toward the front, take the upper corner on the left side, and with the right hand, pull it down toward the waist so that it stays close to the body. Then, gather the right side together and tuck it into the waistband.
This refers to the method for wearing the bathing robe.
The method for wearing the robe when lying down is likewise the same.
When wishing to exit the pool, shake it out and emerge slowly so as not to cause insects to adhere to it.
The ritual for stepping onto dry land is explained in detail in the Vinaya.

If one does not go to a pond but washes within the monastery, the procedure for wearing the lower robe (*nivasana*) is the same as this: one should have someone pour water over oneself, and provide a screen according to the circumstances and the location.

The Blessed One has taught that one may use a bathhouse, or construct an open-air brick pool, or prepare medicinal decoctions for removing ailments, or apply oil all over the body; one should constantly rub the feet with oil every night and apply oil to the head every morning. This clarifies the eyes, removes wind, and brings profound benefit; as there are sacred teachings for each of these, I have not had the leisure to describe them in full, as they are detailed in the Vinaya.
Furthermore, those who bathe must do so while hungry;
only after bathing should they eat. There are two benefits to this:
first, the body becomes clear and light, free from all impurities; second, phlegm and mucus are dispersed, enabling one to consume food and drink.
To bathe immediately after eating is what physicians strictly forbid.
Thus, we know that the saying "wash when hungry and bathe when full" is not a comprehensive principle.
If one wears a three-foot bathing robe, it is too narrow and will expose the body.
To claim that one should never wear anything and bathe in the nude is a profound departure from the principles of the teachings.

One should instead use a four-panel bathing skirt (*snānaśāṭī*) to cover the body in a manner that is both appropriate and pleasing; this not only ensures full compliance with the sacred instructions but also avoids bringing shame upon oneself before humans and deities alike.
Other matters may be omitted; the wise should understand them all for themselves.
Even when bathing at night, one does not alter their appearance; how much more so should one ensure there is no lack of concealment when facing others.
21. Regarding the sitting mat used as an undergarment: when prostrating, one spreads out this sitting mat. This practice is not seen among the people of the Five Indias.

Regarding the method for the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), it should be made by cutting and piecing together cloth; it must be double-layered and constructed with fringes (*pattā*) attached, though the specific measurements are not detailed here.
Regarding the details of what is required: when lying down or sleeping, one should simply take care of another's mats and bedding.
If using another's property, whether new or old, one must always provide a protective cover or replacement.
If one treats it as one's own property, then it is unnecessary; do not allow it to become soiled or damaged by offerings made out of faith, for that would not constitute a true prostration.

The monks of the South Sea each carry a cloth towel three or five feet long, folded like a dining napkin to serve as a knee-cloth during prostrations, and when walking, they drape it over their shoulders.

The Method of Resting While Reclining. In the Western Regions, rooms are narrow and the inhabitants are numerous; therefore, after rising from sleep, the beds are all lifted and folded up, either placed against one side or moved outside the door.
The bed is two cubits wide and four and a half cubits long; the mats and cushions are likewise, being light and not heavy.

Then, having smeared the ground with dried cow dung to make it clean and pure, one arranges the sitting beds, wooden stools, small mats, and so forth, and sits according to seniority to perform one's usual tasks.
All articles of daily necessity were placed upon shelves.

There was no method of shielding the bed with clothing; those for whom it was improper would naturally not lie down there, and as for those for whom it was permissible, what need was there to shield the body?
Regarding the bedding and mats of the Saṃgha, they must be provided with a protective lining to be appropriate for use.
This is the intended meaning behind the use of the sitting mat (niṣīdana).
If one acts otherwise, it will result in the transgression of the "black back" (kālāpṛṣṭha); the holy ones have spoken these sincere words, so one must not fail to be careful.

If one can certainly practice this matter, it will truly sustain the body and further the Way.

Upon both ends of the base, small *caityas* are installed, measured to be level with a person's height; alternatively, one may place sacred images within them as standing statues of Śākyamuni.
If one circumambulates the *caitya* while touring the Buddha hall to the right, it serves as a distinct means for generating merit, intended primarily for the purpose of reverent devotion.
Walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) is a ritual for dispersing [stagnant energies], intended for the nourishment of the body and the treatment of illness.

Formerly, it was called "walking the path" (*xíngdào*) or "walking meditation" (*jīngxíng*); thus, these two matters were conflated without distinguishing between them, resulting in the long-term neglect of this practice for physical regulation in the eastern regions.

This is the ritual of showing reverence to one's superiors.

If any of his disciples were ill, he would personally attend to them, carrying them and providing whatever medicinal decoctions or necessities were required, caring for them with the same concern as he would for an infant.

However, the fundamental principles of the Buddha-dharma take instruction as primary; just as the eldest son of a Wheel-Turning King is nurtured without being slighted, the Vinaya contains explicit statements—how could one possibly allow for such negligence?
Regarding the term *caitya-vandana* mentioned above, it is also called *caitya-vandanā*.

Based on its physical characteristics, it subsequently received the name *caitya*.
Furthermore, it is explained in two ways: first, that all the virtues of the World-Honored One are gathered here; second, that it is constructed by accumulating bricks and earth.
The detailed explanation of the meaning of the character [for this term] is as follows.

The old practice of translating it generically as "tā" (塔) or specifically as "zhiti" (支提) is entirely erroneous.

Next, it says, "Alternatively, they are commonly understood [as such]," which means that regardless of its actual meaning, it is simply based on what people in the world collectively call "skillful entry"; thus, it is a name devoid of meaning.

"Venerable sir, you should please be seated; even if there is to be a reprimand, it will do no harm to remain standing.

As stated in the Sūtras and Vinaya: "Having come to the place where the Buddha was, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side. It does not say that they spread out their sitting mats, performed three prostrations, and stood to one side; such is the teaching.
However, in places where elders are honored, many seats must be arranged; when someone arrives, they sit according to the proper ritual.
As for all those who sit, their feet always rest upon the ground; there has never been a practice of tucking the knees under.

The Vinaya states that one should first perform the *utkuṭuka* posture; translated as "squatting," this involves placing both feet on the ground with both knees raised, drawing up the robes so that they do not hang on the floor.

This refers to the standard procedures for the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification) when holding robes; whether one confesses an offense before another person, expresses respect toward the assembly, requests forbearance after being reproached, or pays homage to the Sangha upon receiving full ordination—all such instances are identical to this.
Alternatively, one may place both knees on the ground and stand upright with palms joined; this is the proper manner for gazing upon and praising the incense altar.

However, prostrating upon a bed is a practice unknown in any country, nor is it ever seen that mats or carpets are spread out for such purposes. To desire to show reverence while instead acting with insolence—how could this possibly be considered reasonable?

Even on a bed or a mat, one does not show formal reverence with a neutral mind; how much less so when paying respects to a venerable teacher or a Great Master? How could such a practice possibly be appropriate?

In the lecture halls and dining halls of the Western Regions, large beds have never been placed there; instead, wooden stools and small benches are provided for squatting while listening to lectures or eating—this is the original method.
In China, large couches and square seats have been used for a long time.
Although one may adapt the formalities according to the times, the fundamental source must be understood.

26. Guests and Old Acquaintances Meeting: Twenty-six. Regarding guests and old acquaintances meeting: formerly, when the Great Master was alive, he personally served as the head of the teaching. When visiting bhikṣus arrived, he would personally bid them, "Welcome."

The guest then follows the sound and immediately says *svāgata*, which is translated as "most welcome.

He immediately takes the bowl and robe and hangs them on a peg by the wall, then sits down in a suitable place to allow the other to rest. Among peers of equal standing, there is no distinction in these matters.

Once his fatigue was relieved, he washed his hands and feet, and then proceeded to the place of the Honored One to offer his respects; he performed only a single prostration, kneeling down to press his forehead against the Honored One’s feet.

Thereupon, he withdrew to one side and sat respectfully; indeed, there was no fixed method established.
However, according to the customs of the Western Regions, people mostly sit on small stools and moreover keep their feet bare.
Since these practices do not exist in the Eastern Land (China), the etiquette of clasping the feet is not observed here.
The Sūtra states, "Humans and devas came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side"; this is precisely the proper etiquette.

If it contains turbid dregs, this [type of drink] is certainly not permitted.

The Vinaya states: "All *pāna* (liquids) must be filtered until clear and yellowish like reeds. This refers to the etiquette for welcoming and receiving teachers, disciples, followers, guests, and elders in the Western Regions.

How can there be one who arrives after braving the cold or comes freshly from the heat, with sweat pouring down his entire body or hands and feet frozen stiff, yet hastily discarding his robes and carrying cases to perform a hurried *vaṃdana*? Such a state of frantic agitation is utterly contrary to the established rules of decorum.
When the Master stands before him and asks about other matters, how truly urgent must he be to consider himself a successor to the Dharma!
Regarding the term "wennan" (和南): in Sanskrit it is called *vandana*, or alternatively *vandanan*, which is translated as "reverential salutation.
It is simply that because the colloquial pronunciation was not accurate, it came to be called "wennan."
One cannot change the old custom; furthermore, regarding "wǎnhuán" (和南), its correct pronunciation should actually be "pàndì" (畔睇).
It is also said that when the assembly has gathered for formal practice, prostrating is not the proper ritual; rather, one should join the palms, lower the head, and recite "pàndì."
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Or again, merely joining the palms, even down to slightly bowing the head," which constitutes paying respect.
Southerners do not examine this closely, following it only vaguely and incompletely.
If one were instead to change "not examining" (*buna*) to "prostration" (*vandana*), this would be entirely identical to the Vinaya teachings. 27.

First, examining the source of illness (XXVII). Regarding what was previously stated—that one should weigh the lightness or heaviness of the body before partaking of a small meal—this refers precisely to observing the relative strength or weakness of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
If it is light and wholesome, one may consume it as usual.
If there is necessarily something unusual, one must investigate its cause; once the source of the illness has been identified, one may then apply the appropriate remedies.
If one feels light and agile yet the fire of hunger burns within, one should only begin to eat at the time for the morning meal.

Generally speaking, early dawn is the time of phlegm; the residual moisture from last night's food accumulates in the chest and diaphragm, and if one eats before it has dispersed, it will result in harm.
It is like throwing firewood into a rising flame; the wood is then immediately consumed by the fire.
But if one places dry grass where the fire has not yet caught, the grass remains intact and does not burn.
Now, "eating little" is a special allowance granted by the Sages; whether it be gruel or rice, one eats according to the measure of one's body.
It is certainly because gruel can support the Path that this alone—and nothing else—is permitted.
If eating rice is necessary for the growth of the body, then eating rice in the morning will cause no harm.
Generally, whatever food one consumes that causes the body to become uneasy serves as a condition for illness.
Do not lie in bed with a headache, thinking it is an illness.
If other medicines do not cure it and the physician prescribes non-timely food (vikālabhojana), the Buddha said that one should give it to him in secret.

While it is certainly not the case that this current differs from that tradition, among the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) of the West, the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*) states: "One must first examine the voice and complexion, and only then proceed with the eight branches of medical treatment."
"If one does not understand this subtlety, seeking to comply will instead result in opposition.

Regarding the "Eight Physicians," they are: first, a treatise on all types of sores; second, a treatise on piercing the head with needles for ailments; third, a treatise on bodily afflictions; fourth, a treatise on demonic fevers; fifth, a treatise on *agada* (antidote) medicines; sixth, a treatise on the illnesses of children; seventh, a treatise on methods for longevity; and eighth, a treatise on increasing physical strength.

The term "ulcer" refers to ailments both internal and external; "head disease" refers specifically to conditions on the head; that which is below the throat is termed a "bodily affliction"; "demonial miasma" refers to malevolent spirits; *agada* is the universal remedy for all poisons; "the youth" refers to the period from within the womb until the age of sixteen; "longevity" means the prolongation of life and long-term preservation of the body; and "physical strength" refers to the robustness of the body.

These eight arts were originally established as eight distinct sections; recently, someone has compiled them into a single fascicle. Throughout the lands of the Five Indias, they are all followed and practiced, such that those who understand them do not fail to receive official stipends.

For this reason, in the Western lands, eminent physicians are highly esteemed and merchants are likewise held in high regard; because they do not engage in killing, they benefit themselves and others.
Having already applied diligent effort to the study of these medical sciences, I have now abandoned them because they are not the primary path [to liberation].

Furthermore, it should be understood that medicinal substances in the Western Regions differ from those of the Eastern Land (China); they are present in some cases and absent in others, and thus cannot be treated as uniform.

For instance, such superior medicines of the Divine Land as ginseng, *fuling* (poria), *danggui* (angelica), *yuanzhi* (polygastrium), *wutou* (aconite), *fuzi* (aconite tuber), *mahuang* (ephedra), and *xixin* (asperagus)—upon inquiry, none of these were found to exist in the Western Kingdoms.

In the west, there are many *kharjūra* (dates) and *harītakī* (myrobalans); on the northern route, saffron is found occasionally; in the western regions, asafoetida is abundant; camphor is produced sparingly in the South Seas; the three types of nutmeg all come from Dvāravatī; and cloves of two colors both grow in the kingdom of Kūlūna.
Only these types of substances are required by the Tang; all other medicinal herbs are not worth collecting.

Generally, when illness arises in this body composed of the four great elements, it invariably originates from overeating, or is triggered by physical exertion, or occurs because one eats at dawn before the food consumed at night has been digested, or because one eats again at noon before the food consumed at dawn has been fully assimilated.
Consequently, this triggered an outbreak of cholera; hiccups did not cease for consecutive nights, and abdominal distension did not subside for ten days.
Thereupon, one seeks the "kidney-qi" of abundant coinage and searches for the "Qin-glue" of high price.
The wealthy may still manage such matters, but for the poor, life is as fleeting as the morning dew. Now that the illness has already taken hold, what remedy can there be!

Even if Lu Wei were to arrive at dawn with medicinal pills and powders, there would be no way to apply them; even if Bian Que were to come at dusk with decoctions and ointments, how could they possibly provide relief? To cauterize with fire or prick with needles would be no different from striking wood or stone; to shake one’s feet and nod one’s head would be indistinguishable from lying prostrate as a corpse. This is entirely due to failing to comprehend the root of the disease and not understanding the principles of nursing and treatment. It is like stopping the flow of water without blocking its source, or felling a tree without removing its roots; as the branches and vines spread further and further, there is no way to sever them. Consequently, those who study the sutras and treatises sigh eternally at the Tripitaka, while those who practice meditative concentration lament longingly over the eight dhyānas.

If those worldly scholars who strive to elucidate the Classics were to halt their progress at the gates of the Jinma Gate, and those seeking the Jinshi degree were to cease their steps at the offices of the Shiqu Library, would this not be a great hindrance to the cultivation of the Way and its practice?
